On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Judges Act, chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide for an additional judge of the county courts of the province of Ontario.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair).

I think we have too many county court judges in Ontario for all the work there is to do. In place of appointing more judges, the hon. minister ought to reduce the number and pay them reasonable salaries. I object to men earning fair or unfair wages for working only three or four hours a day, or less.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The reason it has become necessary to provide for an additional judge is that under the law of Ontario, when a county comes to contain a town which has a population in excess of a certain number, that county becomes entitled to an additional county court judge.
Is this resolution simply to provide for the appointment of an extra judge for the province generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When a county contains a town which has a population in excess of a certain number, that county is entitled to a junior judge. During the course of the year the town of Berlin in the county of Waterloo reached the necessary population. That necessitated our adding one to the number of judges and providing a salary.

Has the judge of that
county court asked for an assistant? Although I cannot go as far as my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) in

regard to the appointment of judges, I think junior judges are being appointed in counties where they are not required, and the senior judges would be quite willing and would prefer to do all the work, and of course get the emolument. The salaries of county court judges are very small; their income does not equal that of a practising barrister of any repute in Ontario. If the senior judge asked for an assistant and said that the work was beyond his capability to take care of it properly, or if the province asked for the appointment of a junior judge, I would have no objection; but a junior judge should not be appointed in a county simply because it happens to have a town of a certain population.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In that particular
county, the conditions were such that, before we were in a position to appoint a junior judge, we found it , necessary to name a deputy judge for a certain period, owing to the state of health of the senior judge.

The provincial law is that a county or a union of counties which has a population of 80,000 is entitled to a senior and a junior judge. There are certain exceptions, such as Renfrew, Prescott and Russell, Algoma, and a few other large districts. Has the county of Waterloo a population of 80,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not the statute under my hand; but, if my memory is correct, a county that has 80,000 of a population is entitled to two county court judges. In addition to that, when a county comes to contain within its limits a town of a certain population, it is entitled to an additional county court judge.
As I understand it, where there is a town of a certain population in the county it is not essential that the total population of the county should be 80,000.
If the amendment was made, it was only reasonable.

I think the minister is right, and that the amendment was made at least five or six years ago. Waterloo is one of the counties in which a new judge
is necessary.

When the memorial was presented to the minister on behalf of the county court judges of Nova Scotia it was pointed out that those judges had more work than the county court judges of Ontario. It does seem extraordinary that they require more judges in Ontario. I agree that, outside the district of Cape Breton and .the district of Halifax, the county court judges of Nova Scotia are not overworked. It is true they are asking for an increase of salary, not because of extra work, but because the cost of living has gone up and because they are not per-Mr. GERMAN.
raitted to engage in any other work. When the minister is proposing an increase in the judges of Ontario, so far as the county court judges are concerned, he should consider the case of the county court judges of Nova Scotia.

Hon. L. P. PELLETIER (Postmaster General) moved second reading of Bill No. 210, relating to Parcel Post.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

Will my hon. friend
explain the principal features of the proposed legislation?

The subject matter of this legislation has been under the consideration of the Post Office Department foi quite a long time. My officers, as well as myself, have devoted a good deal of time and attention to it, having in view the idea that the time had come for Canada to follow the example of nearly all civilized countries and to have a regular system of parcel post. The Bill now before the House is the result of that work; it is short, and speaks for itself. We have now on the statute-book legislation which has been there for some time, and which relates to parcel post; this legislation is to be found in the Post Office Act, section 74. I wish to read this section in order to show the committee that the Bill which is now under consideration does not contain any provisions exceeding the powers which are now vested in the Postmaster General of Canada :
That the Postmaster General may establish and maintain a parcel post within Canada and may arrange with the Government of the United Kingdom, any British possession, or any foreign country, for the reciprocal receipt, transmission and delivery of parcels; and closed parcels, other than letters, and not containing letters, may be sent by such parcel post, and when so sent shall be liable to such charges for conveyance and to such regulations as the Postmaster General, from time to time, sees fit to make.
The Postmaster Genera], therefore, now has under the law the right to fix those rates. The Bill provides that the weight of the parcel shall not exceed eleven pounds which is the Postal Union weight, and that it shall not be greater in size than seventy-two inches in length and girth combined.
The fourth section provides that all charges for the conveyance of parcel post must be prepaid in postage stamps. Section 5 says:
The rates of postage applicable to post parcels shall be determined by the Postmaster General, and all powers which the Postmaster General now has with regard to mail matter are hereby vested in him for the parcel post system.
This, as will be seen, is practically a reenactment of the provisions to be found in section 74 of the present Post Office Act. The Bill moreover provides for the appointment of two supervisors or inspectors, who will have to help us to put the law into operation. In the last section of the Bill we have provided that the Act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council. This is on the lines of the legislation- adopted by the United States, wherein they declared that the law should come into force at a later period; as a matter of fact it came into force on the first day of January of the present year.
We have tried to follow what we have considered to be the best features of the United States system. Other features of that system, while I shall not say that they are bad, have not been adopted, for obvious reasons. We are going to adopt the zone system, but not on the same lines as the system at present in vogue in the United States. In order to be well understood, let me state in a few words how the zone system is working in the United States. There they have eight postal zones, although we may say that they really have nine. What I would call the ninth zone is their rural mail system, to which a special parcel post rate applies. We have been unable to adopt this principle, because our rural system is not sufficiently complete. Their zones have been fixed as follows; The first zone includes all territory within such quadrangle in conjunction with every contiguous _ quadrangle, representing an area having a mean radial distance of approximately fifty miles from the centre of any given unit of area. The following six zones are determined under a somewhat similar plan, each one increasing in distance from the centre of a given unit of area, and extending outward 150, 300, 600, 1,000, 1,400, and 1,800 miles, the eighth zone including all units of area outside of the seventh. Instead of using townships and counties as units of starting points, it was decided to divide the whole country into blocks of imits, each block being half a degree of longitude east and west. There are 3,500 of these units in the country. This is an admirable but a most complicated system which necessitates a great deal of knowledge and a great deal of work on the part of local postmasters, in order to ascertain what rate shall be charged for this, that or the other parcel.

We have thought it much more convenient to adopt the zone system on an absolutely different footing. Instead _ of taking any place in the country as a point around which a certain line shall be drawn to form a zone, we are going to call the provinces the zones, with the exception of the three maritime provinces, which will be for the purposes of this parcel post system, one province or one zone. The other provinces of Confederation will each form one zone. This, I think, will appeal to the committee as being much more workable and much more easily understood than the complicated zone system of the United States. We intend to have a local zone, somewhat similar to the rural mail zone of the United States, but not on the same principle. We intend having a twenty-mile zone irrespective of provincial boundaries. For instance, Ottawa and Hull will have a right to enjoy the rate for that local zone irrespective of whether the mail matter is posted in one province or the other. That will be the first zone, and it will be given a cheap rate. This is done in order to give the legitimate and necessary protection to local dealers and country merchants who have a right to send parcel post to their customers at a lower rate than people farther away, such as Eatons of Toronto, and other big departmental stores all over the country., I met a deputation of the Retail Merchants' Association who came here jin order to oppose this measure and to try to persuade me that we should not go on with it. After discussing the matter and explaining different points, they went away saying that not only had they no more objection, but that they were satisfied with the principle of the local zone of 20 miles. This is the only exception in which provincial boundaries will not be considered, Outside of that, there will be a rate within the province but outside of the twenty miles. The third zone will be outside of the province, and so on until we have reached all the provinces. When we have attained a certain limit, the province of destination will not be counted as a province for the purpose of this Bill.
It must be understood that the Post Office Department does not intend to operate the parcel post system at a loss. I want to have it distinctly understood that we intend to run it on business principles. I am sure that we can do that with cheap rates, and at the same time have the system self-sustaining. If I am not disappointed, I think we may proclaim this l^w for the first of January, 1914, maybe before. There are a great many obstacles which we have tried to meet, and which I think we have met, but there are some in the -way. We have to consider the position of our mail carriers, who now receive a certain remuneration for their work, and possibly, if the mail matter Mr. PELLETIER.
which is given them for transportation is very much increased, we may expect to be told that the former rates have ceased to be fair and reasonable, and we may have to increase them.
Another objection in the way is that many of our rural mail boxes are going to be too small for parcel post. This is a big obstacle. We have considered what we would have to do in that respect, and, of course, there are several things to be thought of. The farmer who has a box might be disappointed if he had to purchase a bigger box. We shall have to devise some means to meet that situation.
The department might do as they do with registered letters-put a notice in the box that there is a parcel.

We have thought of that. Somebody has suggested that the farmer who wants to keep his box as it is, and for which he has paid, should himself put a wooden box or something near the other box, where the parcels might be deposited. At all events, we will see what can be done about it. I was very much afraid that our space in the post offices of the country would not be sufficient. Judging by the experience of the United States, we have come to the conclusion that there is no great obstacle there, because even where there is very heavy parcel post matter at different points, it is found that the parcels come and go so quickly that the space required is quite moderate. In certain localities, however, the question of this space will be a very important one which we will have to deal with between this and the time the Bill comes into force.
Another important feature is the arrangement that we shall have to make with the railway companies for the transportation of our parcels. There is now between the Post Office Department and the different railway companies a good deal of discussion, I shall not say friction, about the amount which the railway companies now receive for the transportation of the mails. I may say that the quantity of mail matter which is being taken care of by the different railway companies has increased enormously. This is due not so much to the increase in the number of letters as to the increase in the volumes called newspapers which are published. We have sometimes been obliged to have special cars added in order to take care of that part of the mail matter. Our friends, the owners of the newspapers, are enjoying a rate which I think we can not call a rate, because it is only a nominal price, onee quarter of a cent. It is only in Canada that such a rate exists. We shall try to deal with this question at the same time that we make arrangements with the railway companies for the parcel post. We

may be able to come to a satisfactory conclusion on the two points. At one time, these difficulties seemed insuperable-these and others which we have settled, and to which I did not refer. Those which have not been .settled will have to be met and dealt with, because Canada is bound to have parcel post. Many suggestions have been made to me, and some people have been very insistent that we should have a flat rate for the parcel post. I must say that 1 am absolutely opposed to that. I believe it is of absolutely no use to try it.
I am now going to give the House a few reasons whien I think will appeal to everyone as businesslike. In the first place, it is necessary, in order to protect the country merchants from being swamped by departmental stores and big city concerns, that a route of certain mileage and special rata should be granted from the different towns and villages throughout the country. It is therefore proposed to give a specially low rate for a radius of twenty miles all around said towns or villages, so that goods may be sent from the rural or town merchants to their customers in the surrounding country. This rate will be low so as to make it impossible for it to be applicable for all points within any one province, let alone on anything passing from province to province throughout the Dominion. Therefore this alone will necessitate two distinct rates, which fact makes against the granting of a flat rate.
The argument has been advanced that inasmuch as Great Britain and other European countries have a flat rate, Canada should have the same thing, but the different conditions existing in Canada as compared with England and other European countries must be pointed out. The British Isles have an area of 121,390 square [DOT] miles, as opposed to an area in the province of Ontario, alone of 260,862 square miles, and as opposed to the Dominion of Canada in its entirety of 3,907,000 square miles, and in this small space, less than half the area of the province of Ontario, there is a population of 44,000,000 of people, as compared with 2,500,000 in the province of Ontario, or roughly speaking, a population of 7.200,000 in the whole Dominion. The conditions are therefore entirely different. In England you have thickly congested rural districts, large towns every few miles, and tremendous cities; in Canada you have a population of less than 8,000,000 spread over a vast area, with few cities or large towns, and with vast spaces that must be traversed where no population exists. The conditions in England and other European countries are absolutely favourable to cheap parcel post, whereas in Canada, owing to small population, vast distances and other reasons already pointed out, the conditions
at the present time are the least favourable for parcel post that could possibly occur. The United States, where physical conditions, area, &c., are similar to those of Canada, present a much more favourable ground on which to make comparisons, and the United States now, when it has a population of 90,000,000 of people, an immense postal revenue, an enormous number of large towns and thickly populated rural districts, in granting this boon to the people has found it necessary to adopt the zone system. If the United States with its immense population and revenue and favourable conditions could not afford to give a fiat rate, it would certainly be much more impossible in Canada, where the population is only about one-twelfth that of the United States and the revenue only about one-twentieth, to do other than the United States has done. As a matter of fact, the system which is now being introduced in Canada gives a flat rate within the confines of each province in the Dominion. In other words, we are giving, as compared with what is done in England, a flat rate in an area twice as great as Britain gives parcel post, and where all the conditions as regards population, cost of transportation and labour are much less favourable than in Britain.
An argument that is very often used in favour of a flat rate is that letters are carried from the Atlantic to the Pacific at the same rate as is charged for one mile, and that if it is possible to carry letters at a two cent rate from coast to coast, it would be quite possible to carry parcels at a similar flat rate, and at a much lower charge than is now made. In considering this argument it must be taken into consideration that the price paid for the carriage of letters, even at the two cent rate, is much greater per pound than the nrice naid on parcels, and to cive a flat rate on parcels it would be necessary to have a minimum charge much higher than the public would be prepared to pay and much higher than the charges which it is intended to make. Moreover, the Postmaster General has the exclusive monopoly of sending letters, and, therefore, gets the carriage of them all; in other words, gets the long as well as the short haul. But this would not be true regarding parcels, as he has in no sense the exclusive monopoly of sending parcels, so that the result would be, if a flat rate were fixed, that it would be quite possible for public carriers other than the post office to get the short and profitable haul by reducing the charges on special distances. It might also be observed that the express companies that have carried on business similar to parcel post for a great many years have never adopted the flat rate system, which they would certainly

have done if they had found it 'to their advantage from a business standpoint.
Australia has two rates, one for each state or province, and the other for the rest of the Commonwealth. The lowest rate is twelve cents or 6d. for the first pound, and six cents or 3d. for each additional pound, within each state. The interstate rate, or the rate outside of the province-or state in which a parcel is posted, is sixteen cents or 8d. for the first pound, and twelve cents or 6d. for each additional pound. These rates are much higher than those which we propose to charge, and there is a further limitation in the Australian parcel post, in that no parcel which exceeds three pounds in weight will be accepted for transmission to any point in the Commonwealth not served by railway, coach or steamboat. Nb such restrictions will exist in Canada, but any, parcel posted at any point in Canada, will be transmitted to any other point where there is communication of any kind whatever. In considering parcel post from an Australian standpoint, moreover, it must be remembered that practically they have settlement only about one hundred and fifty miles from the coast in extreme cases, that large portions of their country are unsettled and unpopulated, and that the towns along the coast are served by water rather than by rail or long land routes, which makes possible in Australia a very much cheaper handling of parcels than would be possible in Canada. The calculation made by the English statistician, Mul-hall, some few years ago in regard to the comparative cost of land and sea service showed the cost on the sea to be about one-twenty-ninth of that for railway service.
The express companies make their charges not on a fixed principle throughout the whole country, but on exigency to suit conditions, where there is competition making a lower rate, and where there is no competition making a much higher rate. This is an elasticity which a government department, such as the post office is, cannot easily indulge in. To illustrate this elasticity in which the express companies indulge in making their rates, the rate between Montreal and Toronto is one dollar a hundred, and between Montreal and Kingston, which lies half way between the two "cities, it is the same. Between Montreal and Pembroke, which is one hundred miles shorter, the rate is twenty-five cents a hundred higher. Similarly, while the rate between Montreal and Quebec is seventy-five cents a hundred, the rate between Montreal and Three Rivers, which lies half way between, is also seventy-five cents.
The only countries that can possibly be compared with Canada, owing to similar physical conditions and vast distances, are the United States, Australia and Russia, and in all these countries the zone system Mr. PELLETIEE
has been adopted, after careful consideration. South Africa, which is similar in proportions and physical features, has the merchandise rate of one cent an ounce, the same as in Canada, at the present time.
In order to give a flat rate, a high minimum charge would be required, and as the major portion of all parcels are sent to places within the confines of the province in which they originate, in order to give a comparatively low rate to a few people at a great distance, the interests of the people who are by all odds the greatest in numbers where the short haul would take place, would have to be materially sacrificed.
The last point to which. 1 am going to refer is this: What are the rates going to be? That has not been definitely arranged. We shall arrange it in the simplest and most intelligent way possible. We expect that five or six lines placed in the hands of the local postmaster will explain to him the whole situation. We cannot think of giving this boon to the people of Canada for nothing, or practically nothing; it has to be self-sustaining. I have here comparative statements which have been very carefully prepared in the department, and which show the rates now charged by the express companies in the United States and in Australia, and the present rates upon our fourth-class mail matter, which is the one approaching parcel post. This is a very long, tabulated statement, and I do not propose to take up the time of the House at this late period of the session by reading it.

The hon. gentleman
might perhaps put it on ' Hansard.'

That is what I was
going to suggest, if the committee is willing. Of course, it has to be done by unanimous consent. I will hand it over to ' Hansard,' so that hon. members will know exactly where we are with regard to our present rates as compared with the United States rates and the other rates that I have referred to. While we charge only 16 cents for one pound, we charge for 11 lbs. $1.76, but the express companies charge only 30 cents. So that the committee will see that our present rates are absolutely ridiculous. They cannot be applied excepting in cases of short hauls and small parcels; and when it comes to larger weight and greater distance there is no comparison whatever. The rates are not evenly balanced. With the unanimous consent of the House, these two statements will be put on ' Hansard.' One takes as a central point the city of Montreal, and the other the city of Toronto. I shall be pleased to answer any question that may be asked me.

subsubtopic: COMPARISON OF EXPRESS RATES WITH THE UNITED STATES AND AUSTRALIAN POSTAL RATES ALSO PRESENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I do not wish to be critical, understanding perfectly _ well the situation in which my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) finds himself at the end of the session, and that the system is, by its nature, very complex, I might say however that his last words remind me of a certain episode. His last words are that the parcel post will be established, that it will be in force possibly on the 1st January next, but that he is not in a position to give us the rates, which by far is the most important thing for the information of the committee. It reminds me of a visit which Napoleon III made to a certain town in France when he was met by the Mayor. The Mayor complimented Napoleon on -his visit and said that he intended to salute him with the booming of cannon but that he had three good reasons why he did not do so-first: I have no cannon. Napoleon said:	I excuse you from
giving the other two reasons. The hon. gentleman has introduced what might be a very progressive measure, but it is only too bad that the country is not made aware of the proposed rates. However, I understand exactly the situation in which my hon. friend finds himself. Credit must be given to him for having acceded to the request which has been made from both sides of this House since he has taken office, namely, that a parcel post system should be established in Canada, as it has been established in the United States, and in most progressive countries on the old continent. I might remind the House that on two occasions I have moved in favour of parcel post, the last motion having come up before this House on the 15th January last. So far, the objections came from a section of the community which is likely to benefit most by the system. The country storekeeper, of course, has always a host of friends around him, he is the mainstay of the village, of the town, and every Tom, Dick and Harry is around his store. The country storekeeper, or merchant, is afraid lest this parcel post would be beneficial only to the large departmental stores. There is something in that objection, I agree, but it is partly overcome by the statement which was made by my hon. friend a moment ago. Section 4 of the Bill says that all charges for the conveyance of parcels by post must be prepaid in postage stamps. That is a convenient arrangement, but it will not permit of the system of accounting which has obtained in the United States, because by reason of their having a special stamp in the United States, they have been.able to ascertain what the actual income from parcel post has been. I would like to occupy the attention of the committee for one moment to quote a few words which explain the position of the United States in this regard. They are contained in a short article taken from the Philadelphia Record, one of the leading papers of the United States, dated June 1, and they will show the committee why the administration of an Act of this kind should be left to the department rather than to definition in the Act creating the service:
Pive months of experience with the parcels post justify the conclusion that it is a money-maker. Two-thirds of the gross income from this branch of postal activity is clear gain, and the estimate of competent observers that'the net profit of its first year in operation will he from fifteen to twenty millions does

not seem unreasonable. The usefulness of a public service to the people is not measured, however, by its dividend return. If it does not adequately perform the functions which constitute its reasons for existence it cannot be pronounced a success, no matter how profitable it may be in dollars. and cents. The desideratum is an instrumentality of commerce that will move to its natural market a potentially enormous volume of farm and factory products in lots of less than 100 pounds, this being the minimum weight for which the railroads will make a rate.
That this potential traffic has not even begun to be mobilized by the parcels post appears clearly enough from the fact that the average weight of the parcels handled by the service^ is about three pounds.
The obvious reason for this is the excessiveness of the parcels post rates. That they are too high is indicated by the net profit of 200 per cent above cost of handling; and for parcels approximating the 11-pound limit the rates are prohibitory, being as high as, or higher than, prevalent express charges. The situation cannot be relieved by any practicable lowering of express company rates; for the companies are compelled by their intercorporate accounting to treat every package as a transportation unit. It must be way-billed and manifested and recorded; the share of each express and railroad line in the total rate must be apportioned; in short, there is as much costly and unavoidable red tape connected with the forwarding of a one-pound express package as there is connected with the shipment of a carload of freight. If the postal authorities had to go through this process and keep a record of every piece of mail the cost of sending a one-ounce letter would be nearly 10 cents; indeed, this is the fee for registration.
Because all these complexities are replaced, in the 'case of a piece of mail, by the affixing of a postage stamp, and because the post office pays for transportation at wholesale rates, this institution can carry merchandise in retail quantities more economically than any other agency; and the post office has command of the only system of transportation which is universal and extends, through its rural delivery routes, to the homes of our more than 50,000,000 of non-urban population.
Moreover, the post office is the only agency that can handle the traffic in less than 100-pound packages at a cost of about one-third the ruling express rates. Congressman David J. Lewis, the author of the postal express law, in a brief submitted to the Postmaster General, shows that a rate of three cents for the first pound and one-half cent for each additional pound, together with an increased charge of one-half cent per pound for each additional 100 miles of transportation, would be feasible, and leave the Government a margin of more than 20 per cent above the cost of service; and he proves his contention to the hilt. A weekly basket of assorted farm products, weighing 50 pounds, could be sent to the urban consumer 100 miles away at a cost of 28 cents-and the kitchen would be supplied at farm prices plus the postage.
This is only an example of the many ways in which a system of exchanging commodities in retail quantifies would tend to reduce the cost of living-and there is ample

post proposition, and he told me of the	long	period	of	inquiry,
examination into conditions, and accumulation of information that had to be gone through by that Country before they were able to propose anything like a well considered measure which would be adopted by Congress or carried into effect. Why is there this sudden development of a parcel post idea as embodied in a measure of this kind? It simply gives the Postmaster General carte blanche to go on. It simply says: Parcel post is hereby established and will be maintained in Canada. That language is very significant. That is the enacting clause of the measure, and the one which, I iassume, is supposed to create immediately this parcel post system; but in regard to everything else, except a limitation as to weight and the payment for the conveyance of parcels, the whole thing is left in the hands of the Postmaster General.
The principle of the Civil Service Act in regard to the appointment of officials especially fitted for the carrying out of this Act is violated by section 6; and yet we are asked to congratulate ourselves in the dying hours of the session that what is said to be an important system has been submitted to us. If a measure of this kind is going to be of any value to the people of Canada it should receive more consideration by this Parliament before it is adopted. I think the Postmaster General should hold over this measure until next session, prepare all the facts in regard to the matter, go into this question fully, tell us what he is going to do, what his rates are going to be, how he is going to maintain the system, and put the whole proposition in a statute, so that Parliament will be able to know just what is going to be done. To say that we shall simply declare that a parcel post shall be established and then let the Postmaster General do as he pleases in regard to it is not proper legislation, and it is not the proper way of approaching a subject that is as important as hon. gentlemen seem to think this is. Why this measure is prepared and presented at this time in the way in which it has been presented ought to have more explanation than has been given. Why should the Postmaster General bring for- ' ward a measure under which he, and he alone, is to determine everything in regard to it? What is Parliament for?

The United States Post Office Department and individual Congressmen gave years of attention to the study of this question in order to frame a well-devised and certain system before they undertook to put it into force. But we are beginning the other way, and the Postmaster General is being congratulated upon the fact that at last a Bill has been presented for parcel post which is nothing but a blank cheque presented to the minister under which he is to do just as he pleases with regard to the matter. No satisfactory results can be obtained from legislation of that kind in regard to the establishment of a parcel post system. I submit that this measure should stand over until next session, but that in the meantime the Post Office Department should prepare all the facts in regard to it in order that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, at the next session, may be in a position to know just how this matter is worked out and to consider and to amend if necessary such proposition as is placed before them, in order that all parts of the country may be satisfied. Any other course will only result in discomfiture. I venture to say that, if the Postmaster General does bring into effect this crude proposition, it will prove largely unsatisfactory to the people, especially under the operation of the last clause of the Bill. My hon. friend cannot possibly frame a measure which would be satisfactory to the conditions in all the provinces of this Dominion without giving opportunity to the representatives of the people in Parliament to declare what their special needs are in regard to the matter. Hence it is that I submit this measure should stand over. If we are to have parcel post, let us have it after the fullest deliberation and examination into the conditions, so that the system will be one that will be satisfactory. To proceed under this Bill can only result in dissatisfaction and in the creation of conditions that will require immediate and continuous amendment. The hon. gentleman, who seems so anxious in regard to his Bill, will be the first one to admit his disappointment. I make this suggestion, in the interests of the proposition itself, that it should be established under proper conditions and with the judgment of Parliament behind it. In the interests of the country, this measure at this period of the session, should be allowed to stand.

speechtext:
I
am very strongly in favour of the Government of Canada establishing a parcel post system, provided that system is established to give the greatest reasonable amount of benefit , to the people for the least possible amount of cost. I am decidedly opposed, however, to the giving of a blank authority to my hon. friend the Postmaster General. The importance of the question of legislating for Canada in regard to a parcel post system, renders it necessary that it should be dealt with by Parliament just as any other subject of interest and importance to the whole of the people of Canada.
I realize that it is the traditional policy of the party now in power to centralize authority in the hands of the Government. We have had many examples of that principle in the legislation of the former and particularly of the present session. This is only another manifestation of that principle. From my point of view the principle is none the better because it is acted upon so often. In fact, the more frequently the principle of parliamentary control of legislation is departed from .the greater will be the abuse and the greater the objection. As a parliamentary representative I cannot be a party to placing in the hands of the Postmaster General the authority that properly belongs to Parliament to regulate a great public service. I would not wish to be understood as making any improper suggestions; but, if I might be privileged to use the word, I would say that the Bill which the hon. the Postmaster General has put before the House is a ' bluff.' There is no provision in the Bill that establishes a parcel post system. It is true that it gives my hon. friend the authority to establish a parcel post system. As a representative of a constituency, I do not think I am warranted in failing to exercise the responsibility placed upon me to see that legislation in regard to parcel post as in regard to other matters is, so far as I can bring pressure to bear, in the interests of the people whom I represent.

In any case, it is the business of this Government in any of its departments-and in the Post Office Department more than any other, because the work of that department touches more intimately and more universally the people in their most intimate affairs-to submit their legislative proposals to Parliament for its consideration and approval, and no department of Government has the right to come to Parliament and ask for such authority as is proposed to be given under this Bill.

To that hon. gentleman I would say that his enthusiasm over this legislation is somewhat premature. When the Postmaster General comes before this House with a schedule of rates acceptable to the people and actually giving cheap parcel post, then he will be entitled to the
*

encomiums which the hon. member for East Lambton heaped upon him this morning. But he is not entitled to them yet. As the hon. Postmaster General himself stated this morning, and as the hon. member for East Lambton knows, there is no more in this Bill than we have already on the statute book. If you read section 74 of the Post Office Act, you will find the following:
The Postmaster General may establish and maintain parcel post within Canada.
The Postmaster General is already clothed with authority in this matter, and we have parcel post actually established under the regulations of the Post Office Department, though established under a misnomer-it is called fourth-class matter. This is provided for in the regulations as follows:
This class includes merchandise of all descriptions, such as confectionery, dry goods, groceries, hardware, stationery (including blank books, &c.) not included in the first, second and third classes, and not excluded by the general prohibitory regulations with respect to objectionable matter. The rate of postage for articles in this class is one cent for each ounce or fraction thereof.

speechtext: How long has that regulation been in existence?

subsubtopic: COMPARISON OF EXPRESS RATES WITH THE UNITED STATES AND AUSTRALIAN POSTAL RATES ALSO PRESENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
For twenty-five years
or more. When I was Postmaster General, I attempted on many occasions to alter that so as to give the eleven-pound limit and the cheaper rate. But vainly; I always found objection somewhere, objections from the express companies and, I am bound to say objections even from some of the postoffice clerks. The only man who was sympathetic was my friend Mr. Ross, the superintendent of the post office in Toronto, who is the authority on this subject in Canada, and who has prepared, to his credit be it said, a long and very accurate report on the subject. If the Postmaster General will follow that report he will come pretty near giving to the people of Canada such a parcel post as they should have. Of course, unquestionably, it is difficult to establish the system. And, much as my hon. friend from East Lambton may say about our not following the United States, it is not a bad thing to have the experience of the United States as a guide in matters of this kind. The one year of experience in this matter which the United States has had will help the Postmaster General immensely in his framing of rates and regulations. So-, we have the parcel post, though under a misnomer. This Bill only states that parcel post is hereby established, but the Postmaster General does not fix the rates. I know it is a difficult thing to fix the rates. I hope that between now and the first of January the Postmaster General will have what the
United States have -had, a commission of experts on the subject. Let that commission be headed by Mr. Ross -and let it include the best experts. There should be no false shame in this matter; there is no reason why even the American postal experts should not appear before that commission and give their experience. When I was Postmaster General, it happened that we had to consult the Washington authorities. Moreover, the Washington officials themselves come to us and consult us on post office matters. There should be no objection to our consulting Washington on business which may involve the department in difficulties if it is not wisely carried out. We had a convention with the United States, and it was so intricate and so interlocked, that, as a matter of course, we had to consult them. Once more, I say that, for my par-t, I have no objection to this Bill. As my hon. friend from South York stated this Bill will be real legislation only when we get the rates. I hope the rates will he cheap and popular. But the Bill is no more than we now have on the statute-book; what we have in addition is the promise of the Postmaster General that before the 1st of January next he will fix the rates.	-

Allow me to say in my humble way that the people of this country are so anxious for parcel post that they would rather take only a fairly good system than have none at all; half a loaf is much better than no bread. I have yet to see that the objections that have been made by members of the Opposition who have spoken are not met by section 5:
Tlie rates of postage applicable to post parcels shall be determined by the Postmaster General, and all powers which the Postmaster General now has with regard to mail matter are hereby vested in him for the parcel post system.

To urge that this Bill should be postponed in order that a parcel post system should be devised is simply to put off the interests of the people-I make no insinuation-it is to put off the just demands of the people of Canada in the interests of the express companies.

The constitutional principle which vests in the Crown the sole responsibility over national expenditure, and which forbids the Commons to increase the sums demanded by the Crown for the service of the state, is strictly enforced in the Committees of Supply, and Ways and Means.

Last evening, it was suggested that the Government should follow the practice adopted in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of providing for representation on the board of directors of the company. It struck me in the course of the discussion that the Prime Minister did not seem to attach much importance to such representation. I desire to urge upon him that, under the provisions of this measure, a situation is created wherein the country becomes a stockholder in the company, and, unless the Government takes some step on this occasion that stock will be entirely without representation upon the

board of directors. The fact that the country is the holder of $7,000,000 worth of stock in the corporation demands, it seems to me, some representation upon the board. The country would not be in a position to have its interests protected unless it had such representation. The policy which was insisted upon in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, in which the country was not a stockholder, has met with results which, I am sure, must have been in the interest of the country, because it enabled the Government to be advised from time to time as to the various internal movements of the directors of the company. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might
say in regard to this amendment, as in respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), that it does not seem to carry the matter farther than it is already carried by the Railway Act of Canada. The hon. gentleman desires an amendment providing that a certain schedule of freight rates shall be filed by this Company, and that the rates shall not be higher than certain rates which prevail by routes partly through the United States and partly through Canada. But in the end his amendment remits the whole matter absolutely to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, as it is already vested in that board, because we find at the end of it these words:
The said rates shall be binding upon the said railway company until further revised by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.	,	) |



So that even if such a schedule weTe prepared and brought into effect by the Railway Commissioners, it might be revised and altered next day. It seems to me that one observation indicates the futility of the amendment. It is not of a permanent character and it has no good effect, because eventually it leaves the whole matter just where it was before. The matter is at the present time under the Board of Railway Commissioners. An amendment of this kind would do no good and it would only tend to complicate the situation. The question of railway rates in the western country has been left to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and on the whole it has received reasonably effective action from that Commission. It may be that from time to time some delay has taken place on account of the enormous stress of work laid upon the commission in view of the great extent of the transportation lines of this country and the variety of the problems that have arisen. On the whole I think they have done reasonably good work, and, at all events, the amendment of my hon. friend does not tend to assist in relieving any situation or difficulty that may now exist.

I would like to say, in answer to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, that there is this distinction created by this amendment, if it is included in the Bill, that there is laid down for the guidance of the Board of Railway Commissioners certain rules that are to be the determining factor in the preparation of these rates. As the matter stands, the whole question is open to the Board to deal with along general lines. This is a definite declaration by Parliament that in the framing of these rates hereafter, in so far as its conduct is concerned, the Board of Railway Commissioners must frame them with this object in view, and having before it the freight rates of the United States, and the idea that there is to be given to the Canadian people lower freight rates, so that we will be able to carry freight from the East on our own soil and over our own lines of transportation. The limitation which, this legislation would impose *would be binding upon the board of Railway Commissioners and the schedules which they would prepare would be of such a character as to give relief and bring about conditions which would be in the interest of the people of Canada as a whole.

speechtext:
The motion which the
hon. gentleman has proposed by way of amendment to the Bill is one which does not seem to me to have any merit or justification inasmuch as the whole question which is covered by his amendment has been entrusted to the Railway Commission under the Act which was passed ten years ago, or in 1903. With all deference to the views of the hon. member for Edmonton
(Mr. Oliver), I cannot see that the object which he has in mind would be advanced by the proposition which he has made inasmuch as the principle which he has laid down is one that is already being acted upon by the Railway Commissioners who are dealing with the subject in accordance with certain definite principles which they have laid down and which must regulate their action. The principles so laid down ought to justify themselves in the view of the hon. member for Edmonton. The hon. gentleman will no doubt agree that it would be absolutely impossible for this Parliament to undertake an investigation into the conditions that are specified in his resolution. The Board of Railway Commissioners have a trained staff of experts to assist them to investigate this question, they have legal gentlemen before them to assist them in the investigation, they have all the machinery which this House absolutely lacks for the purpose of carrying on any investigation of the kind and I repeat that, notwithstanding the earnestness with which the hon. gentleman has advocated his amendment, the passing of the amendment would not improve the situation, but would rather tend to complicate it.

In view
of ail the study I have given to this matter of freight rates, I am convinced that the only remedy is by Parliament laying down principles, the insertion of these principles in the Railway Act, and especially the insertion of the principle of equality of treatment. I do not believe that relief will ever come from investigation on the part of the Railway Commissioners, but I believe that Parliament must direct the Railway Commission that there is one underlying principle governing and that principle is equality of rates. I am sure that if such a conclusion is not reached there will be an agitation for public ownership in this country. If we cannot get the principle of equality in rates inserted in the Railway Act there is another quick procedure and I believe to-day that the quickest and shortest solution of the railway question and the easiest way to bring all the lines within the immediate jurisdiction of this Parliament is for the Dominion of Canada to buy the common stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We have practically built the Grand Trunk Pacific out of the public treasury and we have not control of the road, we have not control of the rates and we have practically nothing for what we have given them except the control that is vested in the Railway Commission. The way to get complete and absolute control of the Grand Trunk Pacific is for the Government to buy in the shares of the company. By that means they will get control of the Grand Trunk railway and Grand Trunk Pacific and by linking them with the Intercolonial railway they will imme-

diately be able to give the people of Canada a transcontinental line that will be dominant in the maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario and throughout the West. I believe that the people to-day are prepared to undertake that venture. It may be that we are only buying back what we have already built but it will not cost a great deal of money to control the Grand Trunk Pacific. We can do this under the legislation which now exists in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. We might be able to do it in other ways, for instance by going into the open market and buying the stock. But the solution is the acquisition by this Government of the Grand Trunk railway and Grand Trunk Pacific, their consolidation with the Intercolonial railway, and then to run that consolidated railway in the interests of the people and with complete control over the rates. It will not be a hard thing to do. I totally disagree with what was said by the hon. member for Welland this afternoon when he stated that he did not believe in the nation holding the shares of a railway company. I do not agree with him at all. We should begin to buy shares of the Grand Trunk Pacific or the shares of any railway wherever we can get them, and we should use them for the purpose of gradually getting control of these systems and consolidating them with the present Government railway.

In offering to the House
this, amendment, I desire to draw attention to the difference in the conditions surrounding the enterprise that it is proposed to aid by the Bill before the House and the conditions surrounding the enterprise aided by the Bill passed immediately before. The aid agreed to [DOT] in the earlier part of this afternoon was a gift of $15,000,000. While the greater assistance is given to the company that was the subject of the Bill of this afternoon, I wish to point out that, according to my judgment, the conditions surrounding the enterprises render that enterprise which is under consideration by the Bill now before the House entitled to greater and not less consideration at the hands of Parliament. In doing so I do not wish to say anything derogatory to the enterprise already aided and neither do I wish to say anything that will unduly or unwarrantably excuse the enterprise that we are now considering for Mr. WHITE (Leeds).

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance drew attention at considerable length, and no doubt with great accuracy, to the enormous cost that has been incurred in respect of this enterprise of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I am not proposing to find any fault with his figures, but I wish for a moment to draw attention to some of the conditions surrouding that enterprise which it appears to me justify to a greater degree the expenditure of the public money that has been expended on it than those public moneys that have been already spent on the enterprise under consideration this afternoon. I desire to speak particularly of that part of the Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise which opens up new country. From Edmonton westward to the Pacific coast, the distance is something over eight hundred miles. For every foot of that distance, excepting such radius as naturally would be tributary to the city of Edmonton; that is a distance of thirty or forty miles, every foot of that eight hundred miles traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific is through absolutely new country, a country that was absolutely unoccupied until the [DOT]construction of that railroad was begun. The building of that railroad has added to the effective territory of Canada an area, served by the Grand Trunk Pacific and its branch lines between Edmonton and Prince Rupert, as a home of population and as a field for the production of wealth, absolutely as great as the area of the United Kingdom. What the actual ultimate value of the territory will be, no one can tell, but that it is and will be of stupendous value there is no question. Every shovelful of earth, every ton of rock that has been moved, has been taken out under conditions absolutely created by and at the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It has been not only a pioneer enterprise, but absolutely a creative enterprise, and while it is to be regretted that the cost is as great as it is, my view of the cost is that, so far as the money contributed by the Dominion of Canada is concerned, Canada is expending that money, not for the building of eight hundred miles of railroad, but for the creation of eight hundred miles of territory, and in doing so, let the figures be as high as the Minister of Finance has placed them, still there is substantial merit in the enterprise and the Dominion of Canada has gained and not lost by its being carried forward.
From Quebec to Winnipeg, a distance of fourteen hundred miles, or, we will say, something over twelve hundred miles, the conditions are absolutely similar to those on the Grand Trunk Pacific from Edmonton to

Prince Rupert, for twelve hundred miles traversing an absolutely unoccupied country, hundreds of miles distant, for a large
part- of the distance, from the nearest productive occupation or settlement. The value of the Transcontinental, between Winnipeg and Quebec, has not only been the building of a railroad; it has been the creation of a country, and as such it stands in an entirely different position, so far as value to Canada is concerned, from the enterprise that we aided by this legislation this afternoon.
Not only so, but by reason of the route that has been taken, Winnipeg, the converging point of the traffic of the wheat fields, has been brought nearly two hundred miles nearer to ocean navigation than it was before. From every side, the enterprise that is now under consideration is valuable not for its mere existence, but for that which it has created. If I may make a comparison, the Canadian Northern Railway Company has done magnifieient pioneer creative work in the prairie West, but the work which it has now in hand, and for which it is being aided by Parliament, is essentially not creative work. It is work which is necessary to the well-being of the system already established. It is desirable from a national point of view, as giving transcontinental railway competition, but it is as a competitor for railway traffic that it is valuable, and not in a creative capacity, as is the enterprise now under consideration. And yet, in dealing with these two enterprises, neither of them completed, and both of them requiring assistance, this Parliament gives to the one of lesser merit a gift of $15,000,000, and to the other a loan absolutely secured.
I have moved, Mr. Speaker, to attach a certain condition to the loan that is now under consideration. I do so with full regard to the aid that the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific is to the development of the Dominion of Canada. But towards that enterprise the Dominion of Canada has contributed liberally, and when we are considering the question of further aid, I maintain, as I did on the former occasion, that that is the time to consider a readjustment of conditions which will secure for our people a maximum of benefit in consideration of the advantage given.
I have heard the right hon. the Premier say and repeat that the amendment I have the honour to offer is not necessary, and not valuable; and I understood him to say that it would not be effective even if it vrere carried. I wish to contend that the view which he expressed in regard to the authority of the Railway Commission, as set forth in the Railway Act, is not warranted by the facts, as we
know them. I do not know what interpretation he may be pleased to place upon the terms of the Railway Act. I am not in a position to say with authority how the terms of that Act, should be interpreted, but I am in a position to say that the object that I have in view in moving this amendment has not yet been attained under the Railway Act, as it stands, and I am anxious that it should be attained. There is no mandate in the Railway Act requiring the Board of Railway Commissioners to equalize rates between eastern and western Canada. No such provision can be found in that Act. I will admit that the Railway Cimmission has power to equalize those rates, just as the members of this Parliament have power to vote to themselves $10,000 as a sessional indemnity. But because they have the power to do that, it does not follow that they are going to do so, or that it would be right if they did so. The Railway Commission has the power under the Railway Act to do many things, but the Railway Commission is governed by conditions and principles that are expressed in the Railway Act, and I assert that the Prime Minister has no right to say that the country is entitled to receive at the hands of the Railway Commission that which I ask this Parliament to instruct the Railway Commission to give under the authority they have. The Railway Commission had power to reduce express rates in the West to the same level as express rates in the East. The Railway Commission took cognizance of the facts both East and West. They delivered a decision which, I am bound to think, was in accordance with their best judgment, and they decided not to reduce western express rates to the level of eastern express rates. Does imy right hon. friend say that the Railway Commission did wrong when they rendered that decision? He will not say so. Then if they did right, when they rendered that decision, I ask him on what ground does he assert that there is no purpose in the amendment that I have placed before the House.
I contend that the fact that this Parliament is giving to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern the aid that has been given out of the public treasury entitles the country to a return upon that payment in rates which shall be equal in western Canada to those in eastern Canada having regard to the extra cost of operation if such exists. That is what the amendment asserts, that is what the people of western Canada are entitled to, and it is a necessity to the well-being and development of this country. When the country is even loaning the Grand Trunk Pacific $15,000,000, is the time to make a specific arrangement with them whereby the de-

mand that has been voiced all over the prairie country during the past several years shall secure the result desired. I am not speaking alone here; I have the demand of the Winnipeg Board of Trade. If the right hon. gentleman thinks I do not know what I am talking about or that I am talking only for political effect, I would refer him to the Winnipeg Board of Trade, a body of gentlemen, who, I think, it may fairly be presumed, do know what they are talking about and certainly are not talking for political effect. If I wanted further authority for moving the amendment I might refer my right hon. friend to the precedent of the Government of Canada in dealing with the Crowsnest Pass railway in 1898, and the Government of Manitoba in dealing with the Canadian Northern Railway Company in 1901. We have a condition existing to-day in the West that calls for a remedy and the fact that we in Parliament are agreeing to provide this money warrants us in securing that remedy.
I move the amendment believing it is my duty and the duty of every member of this House to take this opportunity to provide that remedy.

There will still be a deficit of about $124,000. We are not coming here under any false pretences, and I must throw that charge back at the hon. gentleman. Sir George Ross, now leader of the Opposition in the Senate, when he started this road made an application for a subsidy during the regime of our predecessors in office. When Sir James Whitney came into office he also made an application for a subsidy, and I introduced the same resolution last year as I am introducing this year. The Senate in its wisdom thought it was not right, and threw the Bill out, but they did not hesitate to sanction the subsidy which was granted to the Canadian Northern railway in British Columbia at $12,000 a mile, three times as much as the amount proposed to be given to the Ontario company. This road was started as a colonization road. It opened up a large clay belt in that part of the country, extending into the province of Quebec. The Liberal Government of the province of Quebec has given an extremely large subsidy to the road, encouraging the opening up of the clay belt north of Montreal. I believe it is a good policy on the part of any government to subsidize any province that will have sufficient stamina to develop its own resources as Ontario is doing and has done, and I think it is right and proper that this Parliament should help out any province that will do the same thing. I may say to the hon. member for Pictou that I shall be glad, as long as I am Minister of Railways, any

time that the Nova Scotia Government wants to build a railroad in any portion of their province, to recommend a subsidy equal to this one. When the matter of the railway in Nova Scotia of which my hou. friend has spoken was discussed in the House on a previous occasion, I said to the hon. member for Guysborough that this year I would send a traffic expert through that country to find out whether the Government is justified in making any expenditure there.

I found the contract

vestigations, as my hon. friend is waiting in the case of the railroad from Country Harbour. I take exception to what
my hon. friend says, but I shall deal with his arguments in a moment. This is a subsidy to the Ontario Government in respect of building two hundred and fifty-nine miles of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TIMISKAMING AND NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
If ever a subsidy was deserved in respect of the building of a line, it is in this case of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, if

regard be had either to the enterprising spirit which prompted the construction of the road or to the results which have flowed from its building; results that are not only provincial in character, 'but national. This House is no doubt aware that this road has opened up one of the richest mineral areas in the world. I think that Cobalt produces one-sixth of the world's supply of silver. Then, in addition to Cobalt, we have Porcupine, and in that northern section we have a wonderful clay belt capable of vast development under colonization. A great part of Ontario, some say the greatest part of Ontario, is at the north. If the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern railway had built this line instead of the Government of Ontario, we would not have had the hon. member for Pictou on his feet tonight criticising the giving of a subsidy.

Let me tell my hon. friend that subsidies are given in order to induce the construction of railways:	I
would oppose giving to any company an amount of money after the public got the accommodation which was furnished by the railway.
