subtopic: TIMISKAMING AND NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: I think it is an absolute and entire answer, and I think the people of Ontario will regard it as an answer to the hon. member for Pictou. When the hon. member for Pictou makes the criticism he does to-night, he does not appreciate the condition of public opinion of Ontario in regard to this matter.

subtopic: TIMISKAMING AND NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY SUBSIDIES.
speechtext: Why do you not call the Bill by the right name ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TIMISKAMING AND NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
The people feel that the action of the Senate in throwing out this measure last year was wholly unjustifiable, that the Government of Ontario is abundantly justified in making application for this subsidy, and that this parliament will only be doing an act of clear justice in granting it. Let us take some other cases by way of analogy. The Minister of Railways has pointed out that a line has been projected from Montreal north to meet the eastern division of the Transcontinental railway, ahd parliament gave $6,400 a mile last year to that line, a precisely parallel case, opening up a new territory; and under the administration of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, at a time when I believe the hon. member for Pictou was a member of the House, was not a subsidy
granted to the Canadian Northern railway in respect of a line from Toronto north to Sudbury ? The whole principle of granting subsidies has been in connection with lines opening up territory such as this is opening up. My hon. friend talks about the title of this Bill being a matter of false pretences. We all know that the road is built and that this subsidy , should have been granted years _ ago but Parliament, when my right hon. friend was leader of the Government, did not see fit to grant this aid. It makes no difference that the province of Ontario built the line, if it is proper to grant a subsidy from the Dominion treasury in respect of the building of a line into new territory, the opening up of which will benefit not only the province but the whole Dominion, it makes no difference whether a railway company or a province builds the lines, they are equally entitled to a subsidy and I say it is an invidious distinction and an absolutely unjust criticism to make of this legislation that the province of Ontario happens to be putting forward the claim. If a railway company had put forward this claim no question would have been raised about it by any hon. member opposite. But because the public money of Ontario has been spent, and because it has been a public enterprise of Ontario, the province of Ontario is to be discriminated against, a discrimination that would not exist if the line had been built by a private railway promoter, the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern railway. If one of these had built it, not a word would have come from hon. gentlemen opposite. I repeat that it is a mere act of justice to the great province of Ontario that this line, built from public money as a great public enterprise to open up a great territory, the opening up of which has inured to the benefit of the province and of the whole Dominion, should be granted this aid.

subtopic: TIMISKAMING AND NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY SUBSIDIES.
speechtext:
I submit to
the House, and I invite serious attention to what I am about to say, that my hon. friend who has just addressed the House (Mr. White, Minister of Finance), has not at all placed this matter upon the basis on which it should rest. I grant at once to my hon. friend that if this railway had been built by a private company, and that company had come here, it would have received assistance; but I claim that a distinction is to be made between the treatment to be given to a company and the treatment to be given to a provincial government. What is the reason for this? The reason is that if you do what we are now asked to do, you do exactly what my hon. friend has complained about-you discriminate against the other provinces. We give



subsidies to the provinces already. The province of Ontario this year, last year and next year, will have received from the federal treasury something like two and a half million dollars, one dollar a head of its population. Every year the province of Ontario receives that subsidy. In this the province of Ontario is not alone; all the other provinces receive .equal subsidies in proportion to their population. The Act provides that a part of the revenue which is collected by the Dominion treasury shall be apportioned among the provinces, according to the population. Some of the provinces employ the money in erecting public buildings, others in constructing railways. But, Sir, if one province employs it in constructing railways, why should there 'be given to that province any advantage from the Dominion treasury? It is quite within the right of a province to employ the subsidy it receives as it pleases, but it will be obvious to everybody that if, in addition to the subsidy which you give to the province of Ontario or to the province of Quebec or to any other province, you give further aid from the Dominion treasury, you discriminate against the other provinces. The province of Ontario is a wealthy province. It thought well to go into railway construction. We have no fault to find with that; it employed its own money. But there are provinces which are not so well situated as the province of Ontario, and which cannot undertake, the construction of railways. Therefore these provinces will not do so, and if you give a subsidy to the province of Ontario, they have a right to complain that they have been discriminated against. It seems to me that if you open this door to-day and give out of the Dominion treasury a subsidy to the province of Ontario for railway construction, you encourage the other provinces perhaps to become extravagant, to spend more than they should, and then to come to the Dominion treasury. Railway construction should be the work of the Dominion; but if the provinces choose to undertake it, well and good; I have nothing more to say. I observe that this year again my right hon. friend says there is a precedent for this, because the province of Quebec in 1884 constructed a branch line which is now part of the Canadian Pacific railway from Quebec to Ottawa. The province of Quebec had gone into railway construction, and it had undertaken more than it could carry. The line had to be disposed of, and it was sold to the Canadian Pacific company at a certain figure. Then the Quebec Government came to this Government to be recouped, but upon what ground? Upon the national ground that it Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
had built a railway which was part of a transcontinental railway, a Dominion railway. But, even so, at that time, under the guidance of Mr. Blake, who was then leader of the Opposition, we took the ground that it was not fair to give that grant to the province of Quebec, unless a similar advantage was given to the other provinces?	Was that not right?
Was that	not	absolutely fair? Ifyou are going to give money out of the Dominion treasury to one province-I do not care for what object it may be, whether for railway construction, or for anything else-it is an injustice to the other provinces. You must give them an equal advantage, and, unless you do that, you will always invite criticism, and legitimate criticism. That is the reason why the late administration did not think it ' advisable to give any subsidy for railway construction to any province. The province of Ontario applied to us, but we did not think it advisable to grant a subsidy. We received a similar demand from the province of British Columbia, and we did not think it advisable to give a subsidy to that province. In our judgment, the provinces should be content with the subsidies we pay them every year under Die	disposition of	the British
North America Act. The Dominion Government should not do more than what is provided by the terms of that Act. It may be that at the present time we can do so because we have an ample revenue. But the revenue is not always ample, and, as surely at the sun will rise tomorrow, we shall create a precedent which must recoil upon the Dominion Government at some time or other. That is the criticism which I have to make of the present gift to the province of Ontario. If the province of Ontario were coming to us in the stress of hard times or of difficulties in finance, perhaps we might have looked at the matter from a different point of view. But the province of Ontario is in a good financial condition, and therefore there is no possible excuse for its application.
There is something more. If the view which I have presented does not appeal to the majoritv, there is another point which will perhaps appeal to them. If the province of Ontario, or the province of Quebec, or any other province, chooses to go into railway construction and to build a railway of its own, it is within its rights; I have nothing to say provided it does not come to us for a subsidy. But if it comes here for a subsidy, the least we can expect from it is that it will accept the conditions which are imposed upon a company. If a company were to come here and ask for this federal assistance, we would say: Well and good, but you have a provincial charter, and so

you cannot get this federal bounty unless you accept the law of the Dominion, and make your railway subject to the laws of the Dominion. Is that not perfectly fair and right? If the great province of Ontario asks for a subsidy for a railway out of the federal treasury, it should agree to make that railway subject to the laws of the Dominion, and its tolls subject to the control of the Railway Commission. The matter came up last year, and at that time my right hon. friend objected to that argument, because he said there was already provision in the Railway Act which guaranteed the jurisdiction of the Dominion in respect to the tolls upon a railway of that kind. He referred to section 8 of the Railway Act, which says:
Every railway, steam or electric street railway or tramway, the construction or operation of which is authorized by special Act of the legislature of any province, and which connects with or crosses or may hereafter connect with or cross any railway within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, shall, although not declared by Parliament to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to-
(a)	the connection or crossing of one rail-*way or tramway with or by another, so far as concerns the aforesaid connection or crossing;
(b)	the through traffic upon a railway or tramway and all matters appertaining thereto;
(c)	criminal matters, including offences and
penalties; and,
(d)	navigable waters:
Provided that, in the case of railways owned by any provincial government, the provisions of this Act with respect to through/ traffic shall not apply without the consent of such government.
This provision of the Railway Act shall not apply to the tariff of this railway except with the consent of the Ontario Government. That is the present law; that is the condition of things to-day. So far as through traffic is concerned, our law cannot apply to the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway except with the consent of the Ontario Government. So far, so good. If the conditions remain as they are, the Government of Ontario must give its consent before this law applies. But, Sir, when the Government of Ontario itself comes here and asks for federal assistance, for what is sometimes asked for by a company, is it not right and just that the same conditions which apply to a company should also apply to that Government? The only argument which has been urged in favour of this subsidy is that if it were ask-ed for bv a company we would give it. Undoubtedly we would; hut this is not a company; it is the Government of Ontario, which is acting precisely as a company would ac-t; and
therefore the Government of Ontario should consent or be forced to accept the conditions which we would impose upon any company. So my criticism of this measure is that it is not in the proper spirit of the British North America Act, and that if the subsidy be granted, it should he granted under the usual condition that the laws of the Dominion shall apply to this railway.
Mr. DONALD SUTHERLAND (South Oxford). I wish to offer a few observations in regard to the Bill now before the committee. It is quite evident that a serious offence has been committed by the province of Ontario, in the eyes of some hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken on this Bill, in undertaking to build a railway and then to operate it. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has stated that when this road was about to be constructed the proposition was received very coolly by the Opposition in the legislature of Ontario. He endeavours to make it appear that very little assistance was rendered by the Opposition at that time. I happened to be in the legislature then and I have a distinct recollection of what took place there. I have something to say in regard to the applications that were made at that time, and at later dates for the usual subsidy that is granted by the federal Government for the construction of railways. The attitude of the then Opposition in the legislature was that they did not have sufficient information in regard to the route that it was proposed to follow when the road was first undertaken. I believe that the hon. member for South Renfrew referred to the representative from Ottawa as taking that stand and urging upon the Government the necessity of obtaining further information. As a matter of fact, during the past two or three years, the commission having this road in charge have been endeavouring to overcome one of the chief obstacles to the carrying of heavy traffic over the road. Thirty-five miles north of North Bay there is a very high elevation and I believe that the grade on this thirty-five miles is between six hundred and fifty and seven hundred feet. New surveys have been made and it is the intention of the commission immediately, not only to reconstruct that road, but to build a new road entirely to take the place of this thirty-five miles to which I have just referred where the elevation will be one hundred and thirty feet less. I have the estimates that have been made as to what will be the cost of this road, from which I will quote:
The cost of this diversion between M. P. No. 2 and 35, $1,482,500. Cost of diversion between Dougherty and Temagami is estimated at $367,675, and cost of diversion between! Johnston and Latchford is estimated at $220,000, with additional expenses between M. P. No. 40 and 112 for train filling of $192,935; a total expenditure of $2,263,110.

__ Which justifies the attitude of the Opposi-sSoxi at that time. But later on the Opposi-ifiron urged upon the Government of that day that they should not only build this road, but operate it as well. That was the stand which the Opposition took and it was not a stand in opposition to the building of the road. I have here the record of a question which I placed upon the Order Paper in the Ontario legislature on Febru-mry 3, 1904, and which is as follows:
Has the Government made application to 'the Government of Canada for the usual subsidy given towards the building of railways, to be applied towards the construction of the .Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway?
:2. If so, what reply has been received?
' 3. If no application made, is it the inten-' tion of the Government to make application?
To which the Premier replied as follows:
The Government has applied to the Government of Canada for the usual railway subsidy for the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario' railway, without receiving any definite answer.
They did not get even anything definite from them. Further on he says:
It is the intention of the Government tq -renew the application.
"This was at the time when the Hon. ^George W. Boss was premier of Ontario. He did not receive any definite answer from the Government of Canada when he -made application to them. Applications of that nature have been repeatedly made since that time. I was somewhat amused to hear the right bon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) state a few minutes ago that if Ontario was not a wealthy province, if it was in financial straights, or something to that effect, possibly assistance would have been rendered. We have heard so much about Ontario being a wealthy province and that they -should contribute towards a generous ex-,;penditure in the, other provinces and be derailed similar treatment, forcing the province to do work that should be done by the federal parliament, but when we * come here and ask that even-handed justice shall be meted out to Ontario we are taunted, as we were by the iaon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) who threw out the insinuation-an insinuation which never should have been permitted in this House-that this Bill had been brought in under false pretences and an attempt made to deceive the House. The province of Ontario is not asking for favours from the other provinces or from the federal Government. We are simply asking that justice shall be done to that province and that no penalty shall be imposed on the province for undertaking "to build and operate a railway. I know *that is contrary to the policy of hon. gen-Mr. SUTHEEIiAMD.	I
tlemen opposite. We know in years gone by when the proposition was made to extend the Intercolonial railway westward to the great lakes that it did not meet with their approval. Instead of that they duplicated the Intercolonial, they endeavoured by every means in their power to put that road out of business and to allow the company-controlled roads to put the Government-owned roads in such a position that they would not be popular in the country.
Just a word or two about another matter; that is, the attitude of the Opposition in the Ontario legislature in regard to the Bill that was put through this House last session. We know that it carried by a large majority and we know that it went to the Senate and was rejected by that body. We found that the matter was taken up in the legislature and from the votes and proceedings of the legislature we ascertain that a motion was made by the Opposition there. I am going to read part of the resolution and it is rather amusing. They even assumed that the Senate of Canada did not really understand the question and that the Government of Canada were to blame for not conveying the information to the Senate that this road was constructed. I will read part of the resolution:
And this House regrets that when the question of a subsidy for the said railway came before the Senate of Canada just closed, it does not appear to have been drawn to the attention of the .Senate that a subsidy was applied for by the Government of this province when the construction of the 6aid railway wras undertaken and before the first section thereof had been completed and the matter appears to have been considered in the Senate simply on the basis of an application for a subsidy for a railway, the construction of which had already been completed and which was now being operated at a profit.
They even go so far as to say that it is being operated at a profit. Anyone who takes the trouble to look into the cost of the construction of the road will find that it is not being operated at a profit. This road has cost the province of Ontario upwards of $17,500,000 and we find that during the past year the expenses of operation have increased over $200,000, while the earnings have decreased by $70,000 compared with the previous year. Everything indicates that the expenses in connection with operation will increase. There will have to be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000 expended in rebuilding the road, or in building the road from North Bay northwards for thirty-five miles. Extensions are being continually made. The province of Ontario has met the expense so far .and all they ask is a simple matter of justice. I want it to be distinctly understood that it is justice only

that we are asking for and that the usual subsidy shall be paid to that province. The road will be extended further until eventually it reaches James bay and we will have in Ontario a road which will be a credit to the province and to Canada as a -whole, and which will be one capable of being successfully operated. I rather resent the tone of the hon. member for Pictou in dealing with this question. I do not think it is becoming in any member of this House to assume the attitude that he assumed when referring to the manner in which this Bill was introduced. If he had taken the trouble to read the preamble, he would see that it was not misleading. It says:
Whereas the Government of the province of Ontario has constructed a line of railway known as the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, from North Bay on the Canadian Pacific railway, and at a junction with the Toronto line, so called, of the Grand Trunk railway, to Cochrane on the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and several branches thereof, and has them under operation; and whereas the line of railway from North Bay to Cochrane makes a through connection for the Transcontinental railway with Toronto, and also with Montreal and Quebec, and being, as such, a work of national and nob merely provincial utility:	Therefore Hisi
Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
I do not see anything ambiguous or misleading about that. It is perfectly clear what it is for. It is to remedy an injustice that has been done to the province for a great many years. I think it ought to pass this House without a dissenting voice, and we should at least recognize that any province which undertakes anything of that nature is deserving of encouragement and should not be penalized in this way.
Does the hon. member object that the rates of this railway should be under the control of the Dominion Railway Board?
I presume the hon. gentleman understands that this railway is owned and controlled by the Crown, and that consequently it could not very well be planed under the jurisdiction of that board.

not altogether completed, and it was decided to let the contract in two sections. A contract was let for the section from Country Harbour to Guysborough, and the Sunnybrae branch was purchased. Therefore my hon. friend cannot justify himseli in abandoning the Guysborough branch by saying that less progress had been made in regard to it than in regard to the branch in Halifax. I do not think my hon. friend is sincere when he says that, if the survey had been completed between Sunnybrae and Country Harbour, he would not have abandoned the construction of the Guysborough branch. It is clear to everyone who understands the matter that that was not the reason why he abandoned it. A million dollars was voted to build a road from Sunnybrae to Country Harbour and to the town of Guysborough. There was no question as to survey not being completed. The million dollars in the other case was voted to build a branch in the county of Halifax. There can be no distinction of that kind honestly drawn between them. In the discussion in the House, when authority was given to the late Government to build these branch lines, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was in favour of building both of them. He did not at that time make any inquiry or ask any explanation from anyone as to what the traffic would be. No man knows better than the Prime Minister himself-and he is the man who must be held responsible for the action of the Government in this matter-that the traffic on the Guysborough branch is much more likely to be profitable than that on the Halifax branch. There is one reason that will suggest itself to the Prime Minister if he will look at the matter squarely, and it is this, that the branch which he is constructing in the county of Halifax runs into the forest and stops there; whereas the proposal in regard to the branch from Sunnybrae to Country Harbour is to bring a branch line to a great ocean port which would tap the great fishing industry of the Atlantic coast. There was a probability of shipping coal to Country Harbour from the coal mines of the county of Pictou. There is timber along the line. It strikes an ocean port where a fish traffic could be collected, whereas none of these things apply to the branch which he is constructing in the county of Halifax. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways is very fertile in finding excuses to justify himself in regard to his conduct in this matter. It is quite true that last year, when pressed with regard to this matter, he did make the statement that it would be necessary to show him that the branch would be profitable if it was to be built in the county of Guysborough. It is true also that he did not ask any such assurance in regard to the branch in the constituency of the Prime Mr. SINCLAIR.
Minister. Why is that? Why is the Minister of Railways willing to embark on the construction of a branch in the constituency of my right hon. friend without getting assurance from any person that there is traffic enough to pay interest or even to nay running expenses, whereas in the other case he insists that some one shall give him assurance that if the road is constructed there will be what seems to him sufficient traffic. As was remarked by the hon. member for Pictou, who is to give this assurance to the minister. The minister is the man to find out. He informed us last year that he would make an investigation during the summer and that he would be prepared at this session of Parliament to give some definite statement in regard to the matter. When Parliament met and he was questioned on the subject, what was his reply? He said he had consulted his engineers and had found that it was not necessary for him to make further surveys, but that it would be necessary to send a traffic man over the line to ascertain whether there would be sufficient traffic to pay interest and running expenses. I have already submitted to the Minister of Railways and Canals that if he exacts conditions of that kind in regard to a small branch line connected with the Intercolonial railway in Nova Scotia or anywhere else, he will not be able to get such assurance from any source whatever. It would not be expected that one of these short lines intended as feeders to The Intercolonial railway would pay interest and rrmning expenses at the commencement; it would take some time to work up the traffic. All the minister wants to assure himself is that there is a possible traffic in the vicinity, so that if he builds the line in the course of years the business will be built up. What has been the history of this road in the province of Ontario which is under discussion? Has it not been improving? Is not its revenue larger this year than it was last?
No; less.

I was surprised to hear the remarks of the hon. member for South Oxford in regard to that road. It was currently reported in the province of Ontario that that road was under such good management that it was paying, that it was a profitable line. And comparisons were drawn between the management of this Ontario line and the management of the Intercolonial railway by my hon. friend from South Renfrew, then Minister of Railways and Canals. What has happened in the province of Ontario? Is the road going to the dogs under the present Government of that province? After all, is it not a fact that this railway in Ontario was paying running expenses and a certain amount of interest and with a prospect ahead of it of

paying even better in the end? and is not that sufficient for the province of Ontario? Railway subsidies are not given for the purpose of helping any particular province, but for the purpose of improving transportation facilities in Canada. If a province is fortunate enough to have sufficient traffic to be able to support a line of railway without obtaining a subsidy from the Dominion, and if that road is built and paying running expenses and a considerable sum towards the interest on the capital, with excellent prospects of still better returns in the future, I submit that they have no strong claim upon this House for a subsidy. If they were constructing a new road, we should feel more inclined to pay out public money to assist them. But, especially when they refuse to bring the road under the control of the Railway Commission, I think this assistance should not be given. All the roads subsidized by this Parliament come under the Railway Commission in the matter of rates. That is the principle which hon. members on both sides all agree to. If the Government of Ontario declines to allow the road in question to come under the control of the Railway Board, I submit that that justifies the Senate in the action they took last session.
I should like to have some statement by the Minister of Railways as to what his future policy is to be in relation to branches in Nova Scotia. My hon. friend from Pictou asked him from whom he expected to get assurance that the proposed branch line running throught the counties of Pictou and Guysborough would pay. And why does he. draw a distinction between the constituency of the Prime Minister and the county of Guysborough in regard to the matter? When the Prime Minister, very shortly after he obtained power, sent a telegram to Prince Edward Island a few days before the election, assuring them of the construction of the ferry, and when branch lines were promised to the people of Prince Edward Island was there any investigation as to what the profits of the road would be.

There was a pledge
that had to be carried out.
What?

There was a pledge
made when they came into confederation that something would be done in that respect.

There was no pledge
that there should be a certain number of branch lines built. A number of branch lines are being constructed by the minister in the province of Prince Edward Island. Is he laying down the same principle there v as in Nova Scotia? Is he sending a traffic man to Prince Edward Island to investigate this matter to learn whether these branch lines are likely to pay. I am not objecting to the branches in Prince Edward Island, and do not wish to be understood in that way. But I point out that a distinction is made between the branches in Prince Edward Island and in the constituency of my right hon. friend on one side, and the branch line in the county of Guysborough on the other; and it is up to the minister to show why he is making that distinction.

I argued, earlier in the present sitting, that there should be equality of treatment as regards different sections of the country; and I argue for that equality of treatment in this matter. The province of Ontario has undertaken a work that a railway company usually undertakes for other places; and because that province has built a substantial road opening up a new country- opening up as much country as the hon. member for Edmonton said was opened by the Grand Trunk western section-why should we not have equality of treatment? The whole of that road west of Edmonton was financed by the Dominion; but the province of Ontario built this road, and now* only asks the ordinary subsidy. But, because it is a -publicly-owned road, it is proposed to be discriminated against. Because there is no watered stock, because all the money raised by the sale of bonds was put into the road and the road well built, public ownership is now to be discouraged. There is more territory to the north to be opened up by the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. We hope that they will build a line to James bay and by opening James bay provide a direct way for opening up the navigable waters running into Hudson bay. Yet a Toad of this kind, because it happens to be publicly-owned, is to be discriminated against. What I contend for is the same equality of treatment that I contended for this afternoon in regard to freight rates. There is no reason for the discrimination, no reason if the people build a railway that they should not be as well treated as a company would be. Surely, a province is entitled to equal treatment with a private company. I resent the idea that a road, because it is publicly-owned, should not be treated in the same way as other roads. This road has enabled the great Transcontinental railway for which hon. gentlemen opposite take such credit, to come into operation within a few weeks. The Quebec end is not ready, and the Ontario gate is provided by this very road, and it will enable the Transcontinental to do its work at a much earlier day than it could have done it otherwise. Yet a road that has done this and that opens up a great section of new country is to be discriminated against simply because it is owned by the province-owned by an enterprising people who put their own money into the build-

ing of it. And it is to be discriminated against because Ontario happens to be well off. Ontario is well off. It contributes the largest to the revenues of the whole Dominion.
What is a railway subsidy for?
To help in the construction of a road.
No help is needed for the construction of this railway, for it is constructed already.
I leave it to the people of Ontario to say.
Leave it to the people of Canada.
They are simply asking the same assistance that is given to other roads all over the country.

Suppose I agreed with
the proposition of my hon. friend, that the province of Ontario is entitled to the same privileges as a company, then will he admit that the province of Ontario should be subjected to the same conditions as a company? The hon. gentleman has been a great advocate of control of rates; on that question I have listened to him make many speeches. He has been dinning that into our ears for years. Will he say that the province of Ontario should submit to the control of rates by the Railway Commission if they get a subsidy?
I will not object to that. Speaking for myself, I say I will not object to that; I am going to try to keep a straight line.

Then, how does the
hon. gentleman justify the party he is supporting in refusing to pass the Bill on account of that condition being made?

I say I want Ontario
to be treated in the same way, as far as this subsidy is concerned, as a private company is treated; and if it is in the interest of the public that the rates of the province of Ontario's road shall be under the control of the Railway Commission, I havei no objection to such a proposition.
I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken; he did not decline; he rather did not give a definite answer.

If my hon. friend asked me for five dollars and I walked away without giving it to him, he could very well say that I declined to give it to him. I am not glad that the Ontario railway is not making a profit, but I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that all through Ontario I was met with the statement that if I would run the Intercolonial railway on the same basis upon which the Ontario Government railway was being run, I would have a surplus, as they were having a surplus, while as a matter of fact the two roads were in the same condition: each had a surplus over operating expenses, but did not pay the interest. The Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway is a well conducted road, but the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) brought up a matter which has been called to my attention very strongly. I have communications in my possession from gentlemen along the line of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway urging most emphatically that we should in some way get the Ontario Government railway under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners with regard to rates. If the Minister of Railways will compare the rates on that line with those of the Intercolonial, he will see that, unless a change has been made within the last few months, the Intercolonial rates are much lower. I admit, as I did last year, that there is naturally a certain amount of provincial pride in a local government-owned road; they are a government as we are a government, and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway is a government railway as the Intercolonial is a govern-

ment railway. But when it places itself in the position of a company railway there is some reason why it should accept some of the disabilities as well as some of the advantages of a company railway. As I said, there is some pride in a provincial Government as well as in this Government managing its own affairs, although it does come for a subsidy; but I make this suggestion to the Prime Minister, and I think he will see the reasonableness of it, repeating what I said last year, that the Ontario Government, in asking for this subsidy now, should at least agree, before the subsidy is granted, that the through Tates on its line should be under the Board of Railw'ay Commissioners.

That will be under
the agreement which has been made with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and which has been ratified by this Government and placed before this Parliament.

It might or it might
not. I have read that agreement carefully. The point I wish to make is that the Ontario Government has leased running rights over this line to a company. That company operates a transcontinental line. Unless the Ontario Government agrees that the through rates shall be subject absolutely to the Board of Railway Commissioners, then we have a link in a through line not under .the control of the Board. When I mentioned this last year, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister added the section in the Act, clause 4, which provides:
This Act shall come into force on a day
to be fixed by proclamation by the Governor in Council published in the Canada Gazette.
I think he assured me that before this Act would come into force he would endeavour to make an agreement with the Ontario Government along the lines I had suggested, and he saw the reasonableness of it. That is what I wish to urge on the Government more than anything else, that they make sure that the through traffic by the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other company operating on this line, shall be under the Board of Railway Commissioners, so that we shall have no link in the transcontinental system over which we shall not have control as to rates.

I wish to take advantage of the
spirit of justice that seems to animate the Minister of Railways, who has made an appeal on behalf of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway and on behalf of the Ontario Government, and has based his appeal on strict justice. I invite his attention to a portion of the
Intercolonial traversing the counties of Pictou, Antigonish and Guysborough, and I ask that that same justice which he speaks of be accorded to those counties. The Minister of Railways may not be aware that that portion of the Intercolonial formerly known as the Halifax and Cape Breton railway, was built by a company, and that the municipalities granted a free right of way through the counties of Pictou, Antigonish and Guysborough. Subsequently the Dominion Government acquired that portion of the road, and it is today a portion of the Intercolonial. That portion of the Intercolonial that runs between the Strait of Canso and Sydney was built by the Dominion Government, and the right of way through the municipalities was paid for by the Dominion Government. I say that, as a matter of justice, the counties of Pictou, Antigonish and Guysborough should be recouped the amount they paid out for the right of way through those counties which is now used by. the Intercolonial. Last year a commission was appointed by the Nova Scotia Government to investigate the right of the municipalities to recover from the provincial Government. It was held that the provincial Government was not required to recoup the municipalities the money that was paid for that right of way. The' fact stands out, that the municipalities of the three counties of Pictou, Antigonish and Guysborough paid $200,000 or a little better for the right of way of that portion of the road which the Intercolonial now owns and I say it is not fair that that portion of the road should be owned by the Intercolonial without their having paid back the subsidies paid by the municipalities for the rights of way, just as has been done in the island of Cape Breton. The Minister of Railways says that in this case he has been proposing to give justice to the province of Ontario, as far as the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway is concerned, Canada as a whole does hot own any portion of it; but as far as the Intercolonial goes, Canada and the country as a whole own it. It is only right that as the Intercolonial is owned by the people of Canada the people of Canada should pay for the road and the subsidy orthe costof the right of way which was borne by the municipalities is as much a part of the cost of the Intercolonial as anything else that goes into it, and I say that it is only right that the Minister of Railways should take into consideration the claim that is being made in this respect. A few years ago the province of Nova Scotia made a claim for the subsidies that were paid by the province to the company that owned the portion of the road now constituting the eastern end of the Intercolonial, and this Government,

under an award by a commission appointed for the purpose, was obliged to repay those subsidies to the province. The claim of the municipalities is just as strong, in fact it is stronger against the Intercolonial than was the claim of the province of Nova Scotia for the subsidies that went into that portion of the road, and I would ask the Minister of Railways to give the matter his attention and see if justice cannot be done. When you invoke justice in aid of the Trmiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, the justice of their claim is very faint indeed alongside the justice that is in the claims of the counties of Antigonish, Guys-borough and Pictou in this regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I wish to say a word in answer to some observations made in criticism of the Minister of Railways with regard to his treatment of the provinces through which the Intercolonial railway runs. I venture to say that at no time in the history of this country has more generous treatment been given in respect of the development of the Intercolonial than that which has been accorded by the gentleman who now holds the portfolio of Railways and Canals. The construction of a railway that is now proceeding in the county of Halifax which I have the honour to represent, the terminals which are being developed at Halifax, not for the benefit of that port alone but for the benefit of the whole province and of the whole Intercolonial system, the betterments that are being effected upon the permanent way of the Intercolonial, the provision which the Minister of Railways is making for a ferry from Nova Scotia to Prince Edward Island-in these and in many other respects which could be enumerated if it were necessary, the Minister of Railways and Canals has shown his determination not only to put the Intercolonial urwn a thoroughly efficient basis in everv respect, but also to give the advantages of railway extension in the province of Nova Scotia so far as may be reasonably possible and desirable in the public interest. I do not think that any advantage is to be derived in a discussion of this kind from an endeavour to arouse the jealousy of one province by reason of some proposals in Tespect of another. I shall not dwell further on that, but there are some matters which have been mentioned by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and by my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has taken the ground that a provision of this kind, by way of a subsidy to the state-owned railway of the province of Ontario, is a discrimination against the other provinces. Well, I fail to see the cogency of the reasoning of the hon. gentleman. If this road had been built by an ordinary railway Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
corporation in the province of Ontario, and the subsidy had been granted to that railway corporation, it is perfectly apparent that the argument of the right hon. gentleman would be wanting in any force whatever. If the province of Ontario, instead of subsidizing a corporation to build a railway, sees fit to employ its own funds, or, it may be, to incur a debt for that purpose, is it any less in the public interest that the Parliament of Canada should encourage and assist the building of that railway than it would be if the road had been built by a private corporation. I do not think that the right hon. gentleman has always been true to the principles which he enunciated to-night, because the observations of the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) recall to my mind the fact that on an occasion not many years ago the course which he took was not consistent with that which he now urges. The province of Nova Scotia granted subsidies to the amount of $670,000 to a railway known as the Eastern Extension railway in that province. There was a provision attached ito the provincial subsidy, if I remember correctly, by which the province could take over that line. Subsequently, the province did take over that line, and operated it, only for a short time, and then it was taken over by the federal Government, and became part of the Intercolonial railway. Afterwards the claim was made by the province of Nova Scotia that the sum of $670,000 which it had granted should be refunded by the Dominion. It was refunded by the Dominion, and with interest, although there had been a perfectly plain bargain between the federal Government .and the provincial Government at the time it was taken over which excluded the payment of any such subsidy.
After the award had been made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What was done was this: The federal Government left it to certain arbitrators for the purpose of determining whether or not the subsidy should be paid, knowing perfectly well what the arbitrators were going to determine. That is the substance of it, so far as I remember the transaction.

How could they know
what decision the arbitrators were going to give?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because the terms under which they put it before 'the arbitrators pointed distinctly to the conclusion that the subsidy should he paid back. It was not submitted on the basis of a legal claim at all. The matter was to be determined upon purely equitable considerations, and I do not know that the Minister of Railways would earn any more support on the other side of the House if he left the question of granting this subsidy to the equit-

able consideration of certain arbitrators whom he should select.

If the Prime Minister
will pay some attention to the decision which was given in that arbitration, he will find that the ex-Chief Justice of Ontario based his decision entirely on the fact that the Government of Canada committed a breach of contract, it was for that reason that the money should be paid back.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not examined the documents for some time, but my recollection does not quite accord with that of my hon. friend. My recollection is that there was some claim of duress. It was claimed that the Government of Nova Scotia, having taken over the line, and being unable to undertake its operation, were faced with an alternative which they were in effect obliged to accept, and for that reason they must be regarded as having been controlled by duress, when they did agree that this road should be taken over by the federal Government on certain terms. I speak with all deference to the recollection of my hon. friend; I am speaking purely from recollection, for I have not looked at the documents for some time.
There is another point which was mentioned both by my right hon. friend the [DOT] leader of the Opposition, and by the hon member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), and it is a point of some importance. My hon. friend from South Renfrew said that, I pointed out last year that we proposed not to bring the Act into operation at once. That was not in the Bill as originally proposed in this House. We brought it in by way of amendment and we certainly brought it in for the purpose of entering into negotiation with the Government of Ontario on that point. In introducing the Bill this year, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has placed in it that clause which we adopted by way of an amendment last year, and it stands in that way before the House. It is of importance that through rates should be under the control of one body, but my hon. friend from South Renfrew is perfectly well aware that the provisions of the Railway Act would prevent us from bringing that about without the consent of the Government of Ontario. I do not know what the result of negotiations may be, but we shall have that consideration in mind. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways is impressed with the desirability of it, but he is also impressed with the consideration that in the practical result there will undoubtedly be some such control as that.

When the
Government of Ontario comes here for a subsidy of this kind, does my right hon. friend not think that it should be granted on condition that it agrees to the control of rates over that railway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend is departing from his own maxim of relying on sunny ways. What we are proposing here is not to hold a pistol at the head of the Government of Ontario, but to insert a provision which will enable us to negotiate with the Government of that province, and to endeavour to arrive at a conclusion by the sunny ways which my right hon. friend was wont to practice.

Sunny ways
are always good, but sometimes they are not sufficient.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We trust that under the circumstances, they will be sufficient. Having regard to these considerations, it seems to me that the Bill is a perfectly reasonable provision. I will not go over the arguments which I used at some length last year; probably I shall earn the gratitude of every hon. member in the House by simply referring to what I said last year, without taking up time.

I do not think that the Minister of Railways should altogether ignore the question put by my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm). The cases are very similar. We have not time here tonight to argue out the claim of those municipalities for the return of the money that they were forced to pay to the railway that my hon. friend now manages. But I think my hon. friend should have some consideration given to his request when he puts it before the minister. He has pointed out that those three municipalities were compelled by a local Act to pay a large sum of money for the right of way of the Intercolonial railway through those municipalities. The people were not willing to pay. There is that distinction between that case and the case of the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario embarked in the construction of a railway, and did so wilingly, and they own the road; in the case of those three municipalities an Act of Parliament was passed by which they were taxed. They resisted the tax in the courts, they were beaten and the money was collected. Subsequently the railway was turned over to the Dominion of Canada and it is one of the most profitable sections of the Intercolonial to-day. But the municipalities have not been paid back their money. If the province of Ontario is to be recouped for the subsidy which my hon. friend says it ought to have received a number of years ago, surely the municipalities of Antigonish, Pictou and Guys-borough ought to be recouped for the money they were compelled to put into the Intercolonial railway now owned by my hon. friend, the profits of which are being taken by him to put into the treasury of this country. I do not want to discuss this question at any length, but

I think the Minister of Railways ought to recognize the position of my hon. friend from Antigonish and give him some reply.

The
leader of the Opposition in the Nova Scotia legislature has taken the ground that the claim of the municipalities is stronger than the claim of the province. The claim of the province has been upheld by a commission headed by a former chief justice of Ontario, and the claim of the municipalities against the Government, if presented, ought to be equally successful.

I do not think I
should be expected to express an opinion upon this question because personally I did not know anything about it until I heard it discussed here to-night, but I shall be glad to go into the question during the vacation so as to be able to discuss it with my hon. friend at a future time. I am sorry that the hon. members from the province of Nova Scotia could not support us upon this Bill because we are only granting a subsidy to a province that builds a railway. I said before that I would be glad to recommend a subsidy to the province of Nova Scotia if the Government would only build a railway.

If my hon. friend would turn over the Intercolonial railway in Nova Scotia to the province they might be able to do something with the little branches which are feeders to the main line. But without that it is idle for my hon. friend to say that he is willing to subsidize the province.
Has the hon. gentleman any application for a subsidy for a short line of railway between Antigonish and Country Harbour from the Antigonish Coal and Iron Company?

I do not remember
having received one.
You had one last year, but I was asking with reference to this year.

I do not think I should allow the observations of the right hon. Prime Minister to pass without making a slight explanation. The Prime Minister says that it is only right that the province of Ontario should receive this money because of the large amount it has expended in the building of the Timiskam-ing and Northern Ontario railway, that there is a precedent for paying the money by reason of the treatment which Nova Scotia received at the hands of the Government of my right hon. leader, and that because of the position the leader of the Opposition took on that occasion he is not justified in taking a different position with regard to this case. There is no Mr. SINCLAIR.	.	. i
analogy between the two cases. The Prime Minister will find it difficult to get any precedent for the line of action that is taken by his Government now. There may be cases in the Dominion of Canada where a province has received a subsidy for the building of a railway within its own limits, but I am not aware of any. I would be glad if the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) would tell us of any precedent there is for this line of action. I am sure there was no such treatment handed out to the province of Nova Scotia. I am not aware that any other province in Canada ever received any subsidy from the Dominion for the building of a railway. As far back as 1877 an arrangement was entered into between the Government of Nova Scotia and the Government at Ottawa that when a road was built from New Glasgow to the Straits of Canso the Government at Ottawa would hand over to the Government of Nova Scotia the line known as the Pictou branch which had been owned by the Dominion ever since Confederation. As I understand, the Pictou branch is now the section of road from Truro to Pictou Landing, a very valuable piece of railway, and it was to be handed over to the Government of Nova Scotia as soon as the railway was completed from New Glasgow to the Straits of Canso. The Eastern Extension Company completed their road by some arrangement with the Government of the province of Nova Scotia, the details of which would not be pertinent to this discussion, and when the company completed the road it was taken over by the Government of Nova Scotia. The Government of Nova Scotia came to the Government of Sir John Macdonald and asked for a fulfilment of the contract to pass over to them the Pictou branch and there was an Act of Parliament passed to confirm that arrangement. But Sir Charles Tupper who was then Minister of Railways and Canals refused to consummate the bargain and tlje Government of Nova Scotia was forced to pass over to the Government of Canada this Eastern Extension, because without the aid of the Pictou branch, they could not run it at all. A bargain was forced on the Government of Nova Scotia which was absolutely unfair, but by reason of the Dominion Government's failure to carry out their part of the arrangement' the Government of Nova Scotia were obliged to forfeit this Eastern Extension railway. They were always claiming that they should be paid back the money that was forced from them and, failing to secure a recognition of that claim, they succeeded in having the matter referred to arbitration. Sir George Burton, exchief justice of the province of Ontario, was the gentleman who tried the case and who handed down the decision. His decision is

a matter of record and my hon. friend will see that he based it entirely upon the ground that the Government of Canada had committed a breach of contract in having failed to carry out the bargain and that they were bound to make good the moneys which we lost in Nova Scotia by reason of that failure. That is briefly what took place and my right hon. friend and his Government will not find any precedent in that transaction to carry ofit the proposition that is before the House to-night.

I see there is no varia tion from the usual inspection of a road. Will these branch lines be built up to our standard?

Yes, every branch will cost at least $30,000 a mile.
