On motion of Hon. L. P. Pelletier (Postmaster General), Bill No. 248, to amend the Post Office Act, was read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-mailable matter:
How does section 1 differ from section 9 of the Post Office Act?

I am re-enacting the whole section, for the reason that in 'the French version there are five lines omitted. I am also making certain additions in lines 16 and 17. In line 16 we have the words 'thereof any words or devices.' The words ' devices which ' are new. The words ' in the opinion of the Postmaster General' are also new. The clause now reads:
Any words tending to injuriously affect.
We are making it read:
Words or devices which, in the opinion of the Postmaster General, tend to injuriously affect.	*
The reason is this: My hon. friend knows that the Post Office Department has always tried to stop the circulation through the mails of immoral literature and advertising literature of all kinds of spurious schemes. Now, the Department of Justice have informed us that this practice of ours in relation to fraud orders, which we have followed for years, has been carried on illegally, and they have advised us to have these words, together with the words that are to be found at the end of the clause:
And for the return of such letters, circulars or other mail matter to the senders.
This will permit us to continue legally whait has been the practice of the department for years. We are making the amendment because the Justice Department say we should have that clause, but they suggested the amendment so that we may continue to co-operate under the arrangement we have with Washington to prevent fraud. The hon. gentleman knows that people at the head of lotteries and that kind of thing have changed their fields of operation from the United States,

119ud
where they have been detected, and have come over to this side of the border and continue to use the post office to carry on their depredations. They have questioned our right to hold their letters and to return them, and we consulted the Justice Department with the result that that department said it would be better to get Parliament to make the matter clear.

I certainly do not find
fault with the object of the clause explained by my hon. friend. At present there is much matter passing through the post office that is intended for purposes of fraud. I regret that my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) is not in his place to-night, for he was consulting me some time ago about a	certain French lottery	whose
literature is being circulated in Bonaventure, and I saw the other day an article in the Montreal Witness calling attention to- a German lottery of	which
the same thing is said. Of course, lotteries have a legal existence in Germany and in France, but in Canada, as my hon. friend knows, legislation was passed years ago against all lotteries. The Post Office Department would do well to exercise more vigilance to prevent the letters and circulars of such concerns going through the mails. I do not object to giving to the Postmaster General the widest latitude in this matter, because I know that the power is always used in a very moderate way, and also because of the tendency in certain quarters to use the mails to disseminate immoral literature. It is only right that there should be someone in authority to prevent the mails being used for such purposes. Do I understand correctly that the words 'any words or device which in the opinion of the Postmaster General tend to injuriously affect the commercial or social standing of the persons to whom they are addressed' are to be read in connection with the earlier words in the section concerning immoral publications and illegal enterprises?
Yes, they go together.

Certainly an immoral
post card or circular sent to A or B is apt to affect his commercial or social standing. I see that point. And what was the other point?
Allowing us to return these letters.

Yes. I will give to the Postmaster General privately the names of two lotteries-I do not care to mention them publicly-one operating from France and the other from Germany, sending circulars throughout Canada-

You cannot control that.
Mr. PELLETIER.

I think we can. We
have a law prohibiting lotteries from operating in our country, and lotteries in France or Germany sending circulars into Canada are even more injurious than lotteries whose principal seat of business would be in this country. My hon. friend from Bonaventure showed me circulars into the adjoining county of Gaspe, which I formerly represented, and told me that many poor fishermen have been d frauded by this means. If an authorative statement were issued by the Postmaster Genard stating that lotteries are illegal and that such circulars are liable to be seized, people would be put upon their guard. Also, with regard to immoral post cards, it is simply scandalous to see some of the post cards which are circulated. Many of these, of course are circulated without going through the post office and the Postmaster General is not clothed with authority, nor is the responsibility put upon him, to act in these suppressions of this literature; it is for the provincial authorities to act. But we cannot emphasize too much by our legislation our sense r't the evil caused by such immoral and licentious prints.

I shall be glad if my hon. friend will give me privately such information as will lead to the detection of these irregularities,_ and he can rest assured that we will do all we can to prevent their occurrence. Of course, we have no right to open letters, but in such cases we send our trusted officers to the parties to whom the letters are addressed, and they are requested to open them in the presence of the officers, by whom they are then inspected. We, endeavour to put a stop to anything that is objectionable.

The same is to be said with regard to advertisements for immoral purposes. Many of such advertisements are circulated, and the hon. gentleman can take ample power to override such any gratuitous immorality.
Is it not within the power of the Postmaster General to prevent the circulation of immoral literature ?
Yes.

I have often wondered why the Postmaster General does not put a ban upon the disseminating and sending through the mails by the Senate of the immoral literature they send out from time to time with reference to the divorce cases which come before them. I think we should commence to clean up our own doorsteps first, and if the Postmaster General wants to take the matter in hand and stop the circulation of. immoral literature through the mails, I would advise him to start with the Senate and prohibit

them from circulating the immoral literature which is contained in the records of the proceedings of the divorce cases heard before them.
That is a matter certainly worthy of consideration.

I hold, as my hon. friend knows, no brief for the Postmaster General, but I may tell my hon. friend (Mr. Law) that when a divorce is granted by the Senate, the only copies of the evidence sent out are two copies of the proceedings which are furnished to each member of the House of Commons. For my part, I have applied for an additional copy when I have lost my own, and my request has been refused by the Senate authorities. So far as the Senate are concerned, therefore, their morals are well preserved.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-increase of certain salaries:
How much is involved in this ?
Under this section it is provided that no one will receive less than two dollars a day after a certain date ?
That is it. I am deducting from the $219,000 the $44,000 which we now pay out as bonuses, so that the net increase is $175,000.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-yearly leave of absence with pay:
What is this change ?

In the law as it now stands there is a provision that letter carriers, instead of getting three weeks' leave of absence as other members of the staff do, get only two weeks, and they may be granted another ten days with pay on account of satisfactory service. They have the option of waiving the ten days' additional leave, in which case they are paid two dollars a day for the work they do during that period. Under this provision we are putting them on the same footing as the other members of the staff, and abolishing the ten day period.
'Section agreed to.
On section 8-money for payment of salaries:

Mr. Chairman, I wish to call the attention of the hon. minister in connection with registered letters. Would it not be necessary to amend the postal law so as to prevent the sending of money in letters which are not registered? It is really a matter of deep regret to see
what is taking place every day in our criminal courts. , Under the present law anybody has a right to put money in a letter without being obliged to have it registered. The consequence of this mode of proceeding is that letters are frequently stolen in all the provinces of the Dominion. Children and very young people belonging to good families have been known to so far forget themselves as to steal one, two or three dollars from a letter.
The postal law is very severe, and rightly so, and such employees are punished with great rigour. The minimum is three years, without any option whatever, and the magistrate has not the power to reduce the penalty. Since I am a Crown prosecutor I have noticed that, unfortunately a large number of young men are sent to the penitentiary for the theft of a dollar, and even less.
Would it not be time to'do what is being done in other countries more experienced than we are? Could not the public be utterly prevented from sending money in letters unless that letter is registered? That is being done in several countries.
What countries?

In the United States and in France. I am not positive as to the United States, but in France you are not allowed to send a letter containing money without registering your letter. And furthermore, the person who puts money into a letter and sends it without having it registered is liable to a penalty. Why not adopt that system? I am not prepared to give you the names of the countries where it is in vogue, but I am sure there are several of them where it is absolutely prohibited to put even a cent into a letter and send it without having it registered.
Registered letters are hardly ever stolen, because greater care is taken of them and they can be traced to where the theft was committed; while the stolen letters are almost always letters that were not registered.
As far as my experience goes, it is very seldom that a person is brought before the courts for stealing a registered letter, because thieves do not dare to touch such letters.
I therefore suggest to the hon. minister that he should give this matter his careful consideration, and make a special study of it, and he will find that such a legislation is absolutely needed.
In days gone by it might have been more difficult, because communications were not as easy as they are now. But to-day there are communications with all organized territories, and there is no inconvenience in amending the law in that direction, that is to say that everybody should be forbidden under the penalty of a fine to put even a cent in a letter whioh is to be mailed without being duly registered.

This new system, instead of being a source of expense, will -on the contrary be a source of revenue, and the public will certainly be better protected.
When a letter is stolen, there is no recourse against the Government. You cannot sue the Government and say:	I have
lost money by mail; give it back to me.
I believe public opinion would be favourable to this idea. The losses incurred through such offences against the law are often very small to the individual losers, but the consequences are very rigorous. Now, employees should be protected against themselves; we should diminish for their sake whatever temptations may beset them to take money which does not belong *'o them.
I hope the hon. minister will give his earnest consideration to this suggestion, and, if he does not do so now, that next session he will see that the law is amended in'the sense I have just indicated.

Mr. Chairman, the
remarks of the hon. member certainly deserve consideration, and we shall examine the French law on that point.

I have discussed the matter with a gentleman who is well informed on the subject. The gentleman is Mr. Gaboury, the inspector in Montreal. He strongly approved the idea. He said: You are perfectly right, and he is the man who gave me the information. He said: The thing exists in several countries, and that remark from him was not made recklessly.

We will look into this [DOT]thing. The remarks made by the hon. member will do good if our newspapers endeavour to impress upon the public the imprudence of putting money into unregistered letters, in order to save a few cents or the price of register stamps. The public ought to understand that there are three methods of transmission which afford perfect security; in the first place there are the postal notes, then the money orders and finally the register stamps. As a rule registered letters do not get lost; they are entered in a book or on a detached sheet and their course is followed. Therefore, failing to use one of these three methods of sending money in order to save a few cents is utter carlessness. The money lost by putting it in a letter which is mailed without registration cannot be recovered by the loser , who has no claim against the Government.
I thank the hon. member for having called my attention to this point. I hope the newspapers will not fail to deal with the question and tell the people that they should avoid mailing letters containing money without having them registered.
There is something sacred in the fact that a letter is mailed, but I do not see how we Mr. LAFORTUNE.
are to prevent people from putting money in an unregistered letter. Nothing short of French genius was necessary to discover that means. At all events the matter deserves consideration.
As to the three years in penitentiary for that offence, I must say that the law is very severe; but the * tickets of leave ' abound, and the Post Office Department always insists to have the culprit kept in for one year at least; after that they are allowed to go on a ticket of leave.

It was on the occasion of the investigation I held as a Royal Commissioner at St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary that the ticket of leave was invented. A young man belonging to one of the best families had forgotten himself. For having stolen one dollar he had been given three years in the penitentiary. I felt very sorry to find such a case, and that was one of the reasons why we adopted the ticket of leave. The thing was recommended to the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Mowat. Until that investigation took place the ticket of leave did not exist, and it has been used in order to attenuate such extreme cases as these. I know that after a year or two such convicts are released under certain conditions.

I fully concur with the wise and humane remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Montcalm. As has been said by the Postmaster General, I know that a letter is a sacred trust, which for no consideration should be violated by the postman, letter carrier or anybody else.
Unfortunately, the young men who have to content themselves with the paltry salary of a letter carrier, are often tempted, principally during the holidays-and the Postmaster General will notice that .the thefts of money letters are most numerous during the holiday season-when the mails are much more voluminous than at any other time during the year. Instinctively the letter carrier knows that more money is then going by mail, the young letter carrier whose cupidity is then aroused at New Year's time, when feeling the letters is tempted to chisel out the contents.
I know the law must be severe, but when we come to consider, as the hon. member for Montcalm has said, the amount of the theft, the gravity of the offence and the penalty to which the culprit is liable, it is hard to say how justice should proceed. Here is a young man, aged eighteen or twenty years, who steals out of an envelope a sum of twenty-five dollars or even twenty-five cents-I say twenty-five cents because, right here in Ottawa, a religious corporation who were receiving by mail small sums of five and ten cents had been robbed for a long time before the unfortunate letter carrier had been arrested.

But when such a young man is brought before the magistrate and is sentenced to three years in the penitentiary many bitter tears are shed because the offence, grave as it is, has drawn upon that young man a punishment out of proportion with the offence itself.
I only wish to suggest this point to the minister, but it seems to me that the age of the culprit should be taken into consideration, and that a scale of punishment should be established. It seems to me that a minor should not meet the same degree of punishment as a man of more mature years.
The penalty of three years in the penitentiary is a stigma which hangs on through life. When that young man, after one year, gets that ticket of leave which is given so liberally by the Minister of Justice, the stigma hangs on. He has been convicted, he has entered the doors of the penitentiary, that is sufficient to exclude him thereafter from social circles and to disgrace him forever.
It is useless to insist. The hon. Postmaster General, who has for a long time practised law in the criminal courts, knows that as well as I do. The best means seems to have been suggested by the hon. member for Montcalm. This question deserves consideration, without, however, admitting that the postal service is any worse than it has been in the past. Considering the increase of population in the larger centres, it is a wonder that the thefts are not more numerous, when it is known that millions upon millions are carried through Canada from ocean to ocean. But in the large cities, where the population is getting more and more heterogeneous, the number has increased with the population.
We see every day in the papers that young men eighteen or twenty years old have been sentenced to three years in the penitentiary for that offence. I repeat that three years in the penitentiary is a very hard punishment for a theft which is often very small. That penalty, as I said, is out of proportion with the offence and my hon. friend the Postmaster General should consider concurrently with the Minister of Justice whether that penalty should not be investigated.

The cost of registering the letters might be decreased as a further inducement to the public for using this safer method of transmission of money. Such a decrease would involve no loss to the revenue of the department, for I feel sure that, in such a case more people would avail themselves of registration. That decrease would thus be compensated by an increase in the number of registered letters.
We must also bear in mind the fact that each theft is aggravated by a violation of the secrecy of correspondence. It is found that not only do the thieves take the money I 376
contained in the letters but also read the letters which are often of a very confidential nature. Of course, the letters are not opened with the intention of reading them; they are opened to take what money they contain, but having opened .them the thief takes occasion to read tnem.
I would therefore advise the Postmaster General to reduce the cost of registration so as to induce the people to register the letters containing money, and thus protect at the same time the secrecy of correspondence.

The suggestion of the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) is an excellent one. The time seems to have arrived when the charge for registering a letter should be reduced. It seems absurd that you should be called upon to pay two cents postage and then be obliged to affix the five cent registry stamp. With the enormous revenues of the Post Office Department, in comparison with those of former years, it would seem almost to be obligatory upon the department or upon Parliament to take into consideration a reduction of the registration charge.
How long does a railway clerk serve before reaching the maximum of his salary at the present time?

The railway mail
clerk starts at $500 and goes up by yearly increments of $100 until he reaches $800; and then, from $800, the annual increase is $50 a year up to $1,400, which is his maximum.
Then the mileage brings it up sometimes to $1,800 a year.
Oh, yes, the railway mail clerks on the long routes make a good bit of money.

I have a telegram from the railway mail clerk at Sydney, who seems 'to think that the present Bill makes some changes with reference to the time when a railway mail clerk will reach his maximum. He seems to indicate that, previous to the present Bill, it took twenty years to reach the maximum salary and that after the passing of this Bill he will reach the maximum salary in fifteen years.

This Bill does not
change anything so far as that is concerned, Its only effect on the railway mail clerk is to give an increase of $100 a year to the railway mail clerks who, on the 1st of April, 1913, had been fifteen years in the service.

Have the railway mail
clerks asked for legislation to make the law such that in fifteen years they will reach the maximum?

That is the law now. This clause is introduced to meet in partthe



demands of the railway mail clerks who came to see us. We may not be able to grant them this year all they ask, but we are taking care of the old employees. This will in certain cases put them up to the maximum of their class. We also take care of the letter carriers for whom we are spending $175,000 more than last year. Last year we provided for the salaries of post office clerks. This year we are taking care of the old railway mail clerks and of the letter carriers in whom my hon. friend from Cape Breton takes so much interest. I expect we will be able to do something for the postmasters and little by little meet all the demands, most of which are legitimate, that are made on us.
Perhaps the minister will give some expression of opinion as to the possibility of a reduction in the registration charge.

This is the first time that it has been suggested and of course there is part of the suggestion which is worthy of consideration. The hon. member for Montcalm has put it in very good form, that perhaps it might induce a great many more people to register letters if they had less to pay. But this is a question that I would have to take up with my officers to see what the result would be from a financial point of view. My hon. friend speaks of the large revenue of the Department. Everybody is jumping after it and if we had not a Chinese -wall around it it would be gone.

I was speaking on behalf of the so-called consumer. I am not approaching his revenue from the standpoint of getting any portion of it, but from the standpoint of somewhat reducing that revenue in the interest of the people at large and not of any particular class.

My hon. friend can always take it for granted that the cheaper the rate the greater will be the revenue. That was my experience when I was in his place. When Sir William Mulock reduced the postal rate from 3 cents to 2 cents, it was predicted from this seat by the late Sir Adolphe Caron that there would be a huge deficit in the department. The same prediction was made by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. For one or two years the prediction held good but if the surplus .has been so abundant during the last ten or twelve years it is due largely to this postal reduction of Sir William Mulock. Then, when I was Postmaster General, I made a further reduction in the drop letter rate, that is to say the letter dropped in the city to be delivered within the limits of the same city. Previously the rate was 2 cents, it has been reduced to 1
Mr. PELLETIER
cent. My hon. friend will know .from his officers that commercial firms in cities heretofore had letters distributed by special messengers at 1 cent per letter, which was contrary to law by the way, but was done on such a large scale that you could not pretend to prevent it. Those large firms ceased employing messenger .service for this delivery of circulars or advertisements and became the patrons of the Post Office Department and from that source the Post Office Department has been able to reap quite a large amount of money. I should say that with the large number of money exchanges that are now being made between the various sections of the country by letter, if there were a reduction in the registration charge-and of course in this I am subject to correction by the officers of the department-I am inclined to believe that after a while my hon. friend would derive an increased revenue from this source.
We will look into it.

Particularly would
that be so if the transmission of money not registered were prohibited. If that were prohibited as has been well suggested, and the charge for registration were reduced, I think the revenues of the department would be sustained, and the evils incident to the present practice would be very largely avoided.

The two things will
be considered together.

Under the Bill a person who has been fifteen years in the service gets an increase of $100 a year, beginning cn the first of April, 1913.
But such increase shall not exceed the difference between his present salary and the maximum salary of a railway mail clerk.
That seems to me to put a premium on the mail clerk who has fifteen years' service as against the clerk who has had twenty or twenty-five years' service.

That is to arrange
matters so that the salary will not go beyond the maximum of $1,400. My officers inform me that none of the mail clerks has yet reached the maximum of $1,400.
Has F. N. McMillan not yet reached the maximum?
I am informed that no man has reached the maximum of $1,400. The maximum used to be $1,200, and a year ago we increased it to $1,400, to be reached by increases of $50 a year.

I understand that, but
still it does not seem fair to the man who has 'been twenty years in the service, and who may have reached the maximum, or

who reached the maximum last year, we will say, before the $200 was added.
No man has reached it.
He might have reached it before the increase of $200.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He could have reached the maximum of $1,200, but a year ago the maximum was increased to $1,400, to be reached by annual increases of $50, so that at present no clerk can be getting more than $1,250, or if you add $100 to that, more than $1,350 which is within the maximum.
Under this all the old employees benefit.

I must take advantage of this Bill to bring a certain matter to the attention of the Postmaster General. It has nothing to do with the Bill, but I shall have no other opportunity of directing the attention of th6 minister to it. I wrote a couple of letters to him about it, and on each occasion I received a reply stating that the subject matter of my letter was under 'consideration. Now that wo are near the close of the session I would like to ask the minister, when he has the advantage of the presence of his officers, what he proposes to do about a certain contract in the county of Inverness?
How does that come up under this Bill?
What pertains to the .Bill and what does not, is a question in regard to which I do not require any direction from the hon. the Postmaster General.

My hon. friend
surely understands that we are discussing this Bill, and if he says that what he is about to refer to is in no way connected with the Bill, he will admit that he is not in order.

I simply asked the
right to bring the matter to the notice of the minister, as we are near the close of the session and possibly we will have no further opportunity of bringing up a matter pertaining to the affairs of the post office.

There will be the
supplementary estimates.

A contractor in the county of Inverness was dismissed by the Postmaster General, in the usual courteous and kindly way, before his time had expired, and the Postmaster General kept back the man's salary for the last quarter. He had a postmaster who tried to make political charges against that contractor, and they went to the courts with him. Officers were sent from Ottawa to take him 376i
into the criminal court, and he was exhaustively tried and honourably acquitted. Still, they kept his money from him. I wrote two letters to the Postmaster General to find out why this poor man had not been paid. It was bad enough for the Postmaster General to dismiss him, but surely he should have been paid the money which he had earned. I could get no reason why the man was not paid, and possibly the Postmaster General does not know of his own knowledge, but he is surrounded by his officers, and I trust they will see to it that the little money earned by that contractor will be paid.

I do not wish to be discourteous to the hon. gentleman, who has persisted in speaking on a matter not cmnected with this Bill, tout I may tell him that the honourable acquittal of the man to whom he refers has been reported to me as a gross miscarriage of justice.

I desire for a moment or two to refer to a matter that was brought up by my hon. friend the exPostmaster General (Mr. Lemieux). He says he remembers well that year after year I persistently urged upon him the propriety of reducing the postage on drop letters in the country villages and towns. When he made the reduction in the cities by 50 per cent he should have given us a corresponding reduction in the country; that is, he should have given us a half-cent rate instead of a cent rate. I do not know how the rates aTe working out now under the rural mail delivery, but I am under the impression that we are not even getting the benefit of the cent rate on drop letters. I trust that the present Postmaster General will take up the matter, which I pressed so strongly upon his predecessor, and equalize matters in that regard, so that the people in the country may feel that when the people in the cities are treated so generously, the Postmaster General will be generous enough to give them a similar reduction.
I failed to make an impression upon the ex-Postmaster General, but I trust that the present Postmaster General will not be quite so hard, and that he will do something for us along that line.

If my hon. friend
will tell his people to try that drop letter we will see to it that they are all right.

House in Committee on Bill No. 195, to amend the Railway Belt Water Act.-Mr. Crothers. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair).
' On section 1-short title:

The hon. minister was good enough to give me a copy of the Bill with certain typewritten explanations attached to it. I do not wish to delay the committee. If the hon. minister would make a short explanation of the terms of the Bill, I would then give my views, and the Bill could go through Committee of the Whole without further delay.
The Bill has been revised since I gave my hon. friend the proposed amendments. I understand the Bill as reprinted has been distributed amongst the members.
What will be the nature of the later amendments?
They were made for the purpose of more clearly defining the rights of private individuals. My hon. friend knows the conditions in the West.
That was the only feature of the Bill in which I was especially interested.

Counsel representing
these private interests, counsel for British Columbia, and a representative of the Justice Department had a conference and proposed certain changes. 'They agreed upon the Bill as now reprinted, so that it is satisfactory to those interested in these private rights, to the province of British Columbia and also to the Justice Department.

At this late date of the session, it would not be appropriate that any serious length of time should be taken in discussing this or any other measure that is introduced on the responsibility of the Government. The Government having decided to make certain changes in the law and to place them before the House, these measures must be accepted by the House and the Government must take the responsibility for them.
I merely wish to point out what appears to me to be a course of action in regard to this question that is, to say the least, remarkable. A certain area of land in British Columbia was the property of the Dominion Government. The province of British Columbia assumed to grant rights to water within that area, called the Railway Belt. The Dominion Government also granted rights to water within the same area. The respective jurisdictions of the province and of the Dominion in regard to water were in question. It was decided by the Privy Council that the jurisdiction over the water in the Railway Belt rested in the Dominion Government. That established that rights granted by the Dominion Government were valid rights and that rights granted by the province were not valid rights, in the Railway Belt. As I read the Bill, the Government has seen fit, in arriving at an adjustment of the rights in dispute, first of all to hand over to the provincial Government the responsibility of deciding as to private rights, whether granted by the Dominion or by the province. In the same Bill by which they do that, they specifically establish that right-s granted by the provincial Government shall have equal status with the rights granted by the Dominion Government. I can only say that such a proceeding is certainly contrary to every principle of justice. Rights granted by the Dominion, when the land and the water were the property of the Dominion, were legal rights. Rights purporting to be granted by the province at that time were not legal rights; and a certain provision of this Bill is for the express purpose of declaring that the rights purporting to be granted by the province, which had no legal status, shall have equal status with the rights granted by the Dominion, which were absolutely legal and within the right of the Dominion to grant. If it is the pleasure of the Government to become responsible for legislation of this character, it is not possible at this stage of the session to plead the case at any great length or to attempt to maintain the rights granted by the Dominion Government, and for the maintenance of which this Government is properly responsible; but I do not feel that it would be right to allow the Bill to go through containing such remarkable provisions, without attempting to call the atten-

tion of the House to it. When a Bill bearing this title was brought before the House last session, when the present Minister of Public Works was Minister of the Interior, he made the statement very definitely that the Dominion Government would stand behind the water rights that had been granted by the Dominion Government and, that although the jurisdiction was to be handed over to the province, still the Dominion would protect the rights which the Dominion had granted. This Bill is absolutely the reverse of that declaration of policy.

I readily understand
that my hon. friend has not had an opportunity to read this Bill, although it was distributed yesterday or the day before. The object of the Bill is not at all what the hon. gentleman seems to think, nor does it contain the provisions that toe believes are there. I think he is not quite accurate as to the substance of the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. That case arose in this way: The commissioners appointed by the Government of British Columbia issued a license to the Burrard Power Company to divert a certain quantity from the Lillooet lakes and river, and holders of timber berths lower down the river complained of the diversion of this portion of the water as injurious to their timber limits and called upon the Dominion Government to protect them in their rights. Information was laid by the Dominion Government 'before the Exchequer court and that court gave judgment to the effect that the Government of British Columbia had not the right to divert the water as they had done. That judgment was confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada and also by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The judgment held that the Dominion had jurisdiction in any unpatented lands, but on patented lands the provincial legislature had jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act giving to the provincial legislatures jurisdiction over property and civil rights; and they held that as the Dominion had parted with these rights in the land it had also parted with its rights in the water and that the provincial legislature, therefore, would have jurisdiction. Hon. gentlemen all understand the position in British Columbia. The railway 'belt is simply a strip of land twenty miles on either side of the Canadian Pacific railway right of way, making a strip forty miles wide. Hon. gentlemen know also that the Canadian Pacific railway for the most part follows the windings of the river into which streams flow from both directions. Some of these streams arise outside the railway belt, flow into the railway belt and through it, while others rise in the railway belt and flow out beyond it. On many of these streams are private individuals who have received their patents from the Dominion Government and there-Mr. OLIVER.
fore, according to the judgment of the Privy Council come within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. There were on these streams patented lands and unpatented lands, so that you have a double jurisdiction unless some arrangement were made between the two governments whereby one would administer the water-power. It would be unfortunate and impracticable if there were two jurisdictions dealing with water in the railway belt. The convenience and necessity of some arrangement being made will be apparent to every hon. gentleman who has given the matter consideration. It was agreed upon between the two governments that the administration of the water-powers should be exercised by the legislature of British Columbia, they administering the water-powers and paying over to the Dominion Government the revenues derived therefrom over and above the costs of administration. With that object in view an Act was passed last year but it was found defective in several particulars making it unworkable. We are proposing to amend it in this Bill, making it workable. And if my hon. friend will examine the various sections in this Bill, I think he will find that as far as it is possible to protect these rights, they are protected. All grants and" licenses, and Orders in Council issued by this Government are to be given effect to under this Bill, and all private rights are preserved. My hon. friend will see at once the drift of the legislation; we have endeavoured to preserve as far as we could, the rights of private individuals and at the same time place in charge of the province the administration of the water. You will observe in this Bill that we except from its operations property in all the Dominion parks, so that these matters will be dealt with from Ottawa rather than from Victoria. If the hon. gentleman will read the sections, I think he will find that the rights of private individuals are protected under the Bill. We have consulted private individuals and have satisfied parties represented by counsel, one representing private rights and one the province of British Columbia, and the Minister of Justice representing the Dominion, that all the rights concerned were protected under this Bill.

I read this, as plain as
print can make it, that all records, grants, licenses, Orders in Council, or contracts of, for, or affecting the use of water, which have been granted by the provincial government are given a legal status just as all applications granted by the Dominion Government under sub-section 3 are given a legal status. Both are made subject to adjustment by the board appointed under the Water Act.

I think my hon. friend has overlooked what I have just endeavoured to call his attention to. That is all subject, under clause 2 of section 5, to the rights declared in clause 1 of section 5, which in very plain terms preserves the rights granted by the Dominion or the minister.

It preserves the rights
granted by the Dominion, but it specifically gives the same status to the rights purporting to have been granted by the province as are given to rights granted by the Dominion. The rights which have no legal status are given an equal position before the Water Board as the rights which have a legal status. It is that to which I object, and I do not think it would be right to allow the Bill to go through without calling attention to that view of the case.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House in Committee on Bill No. 243, to amend the Judges Aot. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-Revised Statutes, chapter 138, section 8, amended:
I suppose what my hon. friend wants to do is to get in his resolution with regard to the Ontario judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Mr. Justice Mercier has been a very exemplary official, and has given great satisfaction to the bar and to the public generally. On section 7, judges sitting outside of district, exceptions.

Why is this needed? I know of only one case where a county court judge has power to sit in chambers outside of his district, that is the senior judge of Prescott and Russell. There was some legislation passed in 1907 by the Ontario Legislature permitting a county court judge to transaot business in chambers outside of his district, at a place to be named in the Order in Council. The Order in Council was passed at his solici-

tation to permit him to sit in chambers at Ottawa. It is a great injustice to the Bar of the district. He should come and sit in chambers in the county town, and the lawyers of the district should not have to run after the judge and should not have to come to Ottawa. I would ask the minister if there are other cases than this case-.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The section referred to has no bearing at all on the case referred to by the hon. member. That is a case, as I understand, in which, in virtue of legislation of the Ontario Legislature, the judge of Prescott is allowed to 'ive in Ottawa.
He is not allowed to live in Ottawa, he is allowed to transact business in chambers in Ottawa that he should transact in his county town.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is done under legislation of the province of Ontario, and if I should put into this Bill an express prohibition of that, it would be waste paper.
I did not ask the minister to put in a prohibition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The object of this section is that when a judge is unavoidably absent from his county, laid up ill for instance, he may ask a brother judge of another county to go and take his court, and in some cases it has been thought there were abuses of' that right, entailing expenditure on the country. The purpose of this section is to provide that in order to be paid under those circumstances, the judge earning the payment must make it appear to the satisfaction of the Minister of Justice that his attendance was duly authorized and necessary, that he did not ask to go and take the other judge's court, but was called on by the other judge, and that there was some reason for it being done.

House in Committee on Bill No. 199, to amend the Inspection and Sale Act. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-short title:

Before we make any
progress with this Bill, I would submit to the minister that in view of the protest made against the passing of tins Bill when it was in committee on a former occasion, the minister might very well have with-Mr. PROULX.
drawn it. It appears to me more than ever that the only people who are going to benefit by the passing of this Bill are the already privileged class of the fruit growers in British Columbia and possibly, to .some extent, the fruit growers of other provinces. I am confirmed in that opinion by a despatch which came to my notice some days ago, dated Winnipeg, May 15, in which a gentleman of that city, Mr. George Grisdale, president of the Winnipeg Wholesale Fruit Jobbers Association, expressed the following opinion with reference to this legislation:
Winnipeg, May 15.-Geo. Grisdale, speaking as president of the Winnipeg Wholesale Fruit Jobbers Association, stated that the change made by amendment to the Canadian Fruits Act was an attempt to cater to the fruit growers of British Columbia and Ontario by restricting importation from the United States to the West, but United States dealers do both their packing and grading so well that the public demands their goods.
'Before the fruit growers of British Columbia and Ontario,' said Mr. Grisdale. ' can stop the importation of fruit from the South they will have to cultivate their trees better and look more to their grading and packing than they have done in the past. Then, again, Canadian fruit and that from the Uniteld States is not ready for the market at the same time and it is necessary to get fruit from the South before Canadian fruit comes in.'
The substance of this Bill is contained in the second section which provides:
The Governor in Council, by regulation, mayfa) prescribe- the kinds of imported fruit the packages containing which must be branded or marked;
(b)	prescribe the brands or marks to be
used thereon;
(c)	prescribe the manner and places in and
at which such fruit is to be inspected and such packages branded or marked.
All packages of fruit not branded or marked in accordance with such regulations shall be forfeited to His Majesty, and may be destroyed or otherwise disposed of as the minister may direct.
I do not know Mr. Grisdale personally, but he is a man in the fruit business who imports a great deal of fruit apparently from the United States, as do all fruit jobbers and wholesalers throughout the West and throughout the country. If the minister has a fear that fruit is coming in from the United States of an inferior quality, that it is not properly branded or graded and that the people are being defrauded by the methods of grading and branding of the fruit growers of the United States, Mr. Grisdale's opinion would be that the minister is mistaken in that because he says that the grading of fruit in the United States occupies a higher position than in Canada, and that the fruit imported from the United States is, apparently, on an average, better graded than

the fruit in Canada and is of better quality. That is to say they live up better to their regulation and he complains of the way in which the packing of fruit is done in Canada and in which Canadian fruit growers live up to the Fruit Marking Act and the regulations made under it. The minister did not say, on the former occasion, that there was any demand whatever on the part of the consumers throughout Canada for this legislation. After reading the opinion of one whose business is the fruit business, I am more than ever confirmed in my view that the only class who will be benefited by this legislation are the fruit growers of British Columbia and of	other	parts of	Canada.
I fancy that so far as other parts of Canada are concerned, they are a negligible quantity, and that the protest comes from the fruit growers of British Columbia. It is at the behest of the fruit growers of British Columbia, and for their benefit, that the minister has introduced this legislation. If he had shown us that the United States exporters of fruit were making it a practice to send into this country fruit improperly marked, branded or graded, there might be some show of justification for this legislation. The tariff protects the fruit growers of British Columbia, and that ought to be sufficient. But, in his legislation, the minister certainly takes to himself the power to practically prohibit the importation of fruit from the outside. Now, why should that be? Why should the Minister of Agriculture or any other person have that power? The Canadian exporter of apples or of other fruits would regard it as a very grievous hardship indeed if other countries to which he exports were to apply legislation of this kind. I think that this is class legislation, and that it is exceedingly objectionable from the point of view of the great consuming population of this country, and especially of the people on the plains, where we do not grow to any extent the larger fruits such as apples. There is no question of doubt that the more regulations of this kind that we have, the more expensive will fruit be for the consumer. Take for instance the case of the fruit grower in the State of Washington or in any of the States contiguous to western Canada. Under this legislation, the minister takes to himself the right to-

prescribe the kinds of imported fruits the packages containing which must be branded or marked, to prescribe the brands or marks1 to be used thereon.
We quite understand that under our regulations the Canadian fruit grower is compelled to grade his fruit according to the regulations and according to the terms of the Act. The brands used by the fruit
growers and packers in the United States aTe distinct from outs. They do not use the same names, and there is some slight variation in the grades. For instance, our No. 1 may approximate to a similar grade or brand in the United States, but there is a slight difference. Supposing that a wholesale merchant in the city of Winnipeg sends an order to a shipper in the State of Washington. That order is received, and what is the consequence? That particular exporter has his fruit packed and branded according to the legislation of the State of Washington. If the Minister of Agriculture compels that fruit grower or shipper to conform to regulations which he may lay down for fruits coming into Canada, that exporter in the city of Washington will be compelled to take the fruit out of the packages in which he had placed it, and re-select, and regrade, and re-mark it according to the regulations imposed by our legislation. What is the result going to be to the consumers? The only possible result from that sort of thing is that if the exporter in the State of Washington or in any other state to the south of us, is compelled to go to this trouble in filling an order from a Canadian importer, the price will necessarily be enhanced. That can be the only possible result. I repeat that the condition will be particularly onerous in view of the fact that, as Mr. Grisdale states, the seasons in the two countries vary. The fruit to the south matures before the fruit in the province of British Columbia, and I think that that in itself, along with the tariff ought to he quite sufficient protection for the fruit growers of that province. I would like to hear from the minister whether in view of these considerations he does not think it would be advisable to withdraw this Bill.

Before the minister replies, I wish to enter my protect against this Bill. I shall do so briefly, as I gave my views on the second reading. I look upon it as the most vicious legislation which has been introduced during this session, and that is saying a good deal. There is one point which perhaps my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) did not emphasize. I do not say that the minister will do all that is proposed to be done under this legislation, but this Parliament is not acting properly when it places in the hands of any minister such powers as the Minister of Agriculture is asking under this Bill. All he has to do is to prescribe by regulation that a certain brand shall be placed upon those goods, contrary to the law of the country in which it is produced, and he absolutely prohibits the importation of those goods into Canada.

In the United States, they have their Inspection and Sales Act just as we have in Canada. Their law provides that the fruit shall be inspected and branded in a certain way, and the moment my hon. friend prescribes regulations different from those, he prohibits the importation of those goods into Canada. To my mind that is the real difficulty in the matter, and I rather think it is the real object of this legislation. Look at the enormous powers he is asking.
The Governor in Council by regulation may prescribe the kinds of imported fruits, the packages containing which must be branded or marked.
In the first place he can say that every article of fruit that comes into Canada must be branded or marked. Next he can-
-prescribe the brands or marks to be used thereon.
Then he can-

prescribe the manner and places in and at which such fruit is to he inspected, and such packages branded or marked.
It may be interesting to some members of the committee to realize the enormous quantities of fruit which we bring into Canada from the United States every year. We have to bring it in because our fruit is not matured at the time the United States fruit is. I have 'here the trade and navigation returns for the first eleven months of the last fiscal year, and I find that during that period we imported from the United States $751,000 worth of green apples. We would not bring these apples into this country unless we needed them, and I think it is fair to assume that they would not be imported if we produced them for our own consumption at that particular time. They were brought in because we had to have them. Take blackberries, gooseberries, raspberries, and strawberries, $565,000 worth came in; cherries $102,000 worth and we know that these cherries are brought in here before our cherries are ripe for the market; grapes from the United States, $279,000 worth; peaches from the United States, $330,000; plums from the United States, $266,000 worth; quinces, apricots, pears and nectarines, $372,000 worth. There is nothing coming from any other country practically than the United States. Our total importations, with the exception of a mere bagatelle, come from the United States. All the minister has to do under this law is to prescribe a mark or brand different from that prescribed by the law of the United States and we prohibit the importation of these goods. Surely, if the protection which the tariff gives is not sufficient for the fruit-growers of Canada, they had better go out of business, the country had better pension them off and the land Mr. CARVELL.
which they occupy had better be devoted to some ether purpose. If the labouring men and consumers of this country have to pay any more for their fruit than they are paying now the country had better pension off the _ fruit-growers, keep them out of this business, and let them devote their energies to something else. This :is class legislation of the most vicious kind; legislation that is not justified, that is a direct attack on the labouring and consuming people of the country and entirely in the interests of the fruit-growers in two or three sections of the Dominion.

I can only assure my hon, friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) that the purpose of this Bill is simply to establish uniformity in the grading, packing and branding of all fruits that are sold in Canada. A man who offers a case of apples in Canada shall offer it under certain markings and grades that are prescribed by this Act whether he is a foreign producer or a home producer. I will be frank with my hon. friend and say that there is not the faintest possibility of the Government dealing with the various foreign fruits that he has mentioned, or that he mentioned the other day, because it would be folly on the Government's part or on the department's part to antagonize people in Canada by dealing with those things that we do not grow at all.
Do we not grow apples, pears, peaches, plums and cherries?

There is a great deal of foreign fruit that we do not grow here at all. I am only saying that this provision will only be applied to some of the deciduous fruits that we grow and the Act, as it stood, which is practically as the Act stands now except that the Justice Department thought that we should have it made clearer, has been applied to some extent, because there have been prosecutions against producers of or dealers in fruit that has been shipped in as violating the terms of the old Act. But when we came to apply the Act to the packers of the fruit it could not be applied in the same way as to the home packers, because the people who were the packers were on the other side of the line. This amendment will not necessarily restrict the sale of American fruit. The American producer who sends fruit to Canada, after this is published in the Canada Gazette, will know what the requirements are as to branding in this country and will conform to them. I cheerfully admit, what was stated by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely), that an immense amount of American fruit comes packed in first-class style, is admirable in every respect, and that no person in British Columbia

can criticise it. But if that he true it is also the fact that occasionally fruit does come in that is misleading as to the brand and this proposed law will put it on the same basis as that occupied by Canadian fruit. All that is aimed at by this amendment is to put everybody on the same footing with respect to the Act.

If that is all my hon. friend wants, why does he not provide that the Governor in Council may take power to prescribe places at which this fruit may be branded? My hon. friend says that it is well packed and properly branded now. Why does he want to provide places? If he provides places he prohibits the importation of fruit except through those places.
It is quite evident that we could not provide that the fruit shall be branded in Washington or Oregon or New York because we have no jurisdiction there.
Thas is what we object to.

We have only jurisdiction to deal with it in this country, it has to be inspected at a custom point and the intention of the act is that it shall be put on the same footing as any other fruit. That is the whole purpose of the enactment. We cannot say that a man shall brand his fruit in some obscure place in Oregon, Washington, New York or Florida. We can only deal with it after it comes into this country and then we say that it shall conform to our law. My hon. friend asked the reason for establishing these regulations. If he were to ship any commodity to the United States he would have to conform to their regulations. If he were to ship the finest carcass of beef to the United States it would only be admitted under certain conditions. In regard to a great many things you must conform to the regulations of the country to which you ship them and they will not ibe admitted unless you comply with these conditions. I assure my hon. friend that there is absolutely no desire under the provisions of this bill on the part of my department to do anything but apply to some deciduous fruits the same grades that are establised by this act and there is no desire to work any hardship. We are simply providing for the possibility of some one undertaking to sell fruit purporting to be of a certain brand when as a matter of fact it does not conform to that standard. If we say to our own Canadian citizen: You must mark your fruit as being of a certain grade and you shall not put any other brand upon your fruit, surely my hon. friend would not expect that we would ask for anything less from the man who undertakes to sell the same kind of foreign fruit in our markets.

I must take my hon.
friend's word when he says that he is not trying to prevent the importation of fruit from foreign countries but my hon. friend has admitted all that we have been trying to argue. He has told us that branding will not take place in the United States but has to take place at certain designated points in Canada. That is the very thing we are objecting to. I just want to give him a concrete illustration of what will be done. The law provides that strawberries must be branded in a certain way and that they must be branded when they get into Canada. The strawberries will be held at Vanceboro or Macadam Junction on the New Brunswick frontier until they are rotten and the Canadian consumer will be prevented from getting them. It will be the same with peaches. They are stopped at the boundary line and they will be rotten before they can get to their destination. My hon. friend says: Trust me. Yes, I will trust my hon. friend, but he will not always be the minister of Agriculture. That may be possible, and we have to' guard against all these possibilities. We are objecting to my hon. friend making legislation by which a man, who has not his ideas of fair-play and uprightness between man and man, would have the right to injure the public. My hon. friend has confessed all we are claiming, namely: that this legislation is giving him rights which no government should have. It is interfering with the liberty of the subject and the very living of the people.

My hon. friend has made the plea that the present Act is not sufficient. In my humble judgment the present Act is sufficient if protection to the consumer is all that is wanted. Section 320 provides for the marking of fruit; that is to say, it lays down a certain law which governs the Canadian producer of fruit for market. Section 321 lays down the rules which shall govern the condition of foreign fruit offered for sale in Canada. I maintain that the provisions of section 321 are entirely adequate to give all necessary protection to the consumer. The provisions are naturally of a general character; but their result is that fruit must be sound, honestly packed and honestly branded. My hon. friend needs no more authority to protect the Canadian consumer of foreign fruit than is contained in that section. When he asks for legislation to place in his hands authority whereby, as has certainly been proved by my hon. friends who have already spoken, not only can he prevent the importation of foreign fruit into Canada, or hamper the importation to such a degree as to minimize the advantage of its importation; but, if he puts this law on the statute-book, he will be required to take action under it, either that or the law should not be on the

statute-book. The plea of fair-dealing that my hon. friend makes in his own behalf does not hold good. He is asking for legislation that is not necessary, that, if it is enforced, will be seriously detrimental to the country; and that, if it is put on the statute-book, it will be his responsibility to enforce. In the face of that condition, I certainly wish to enter my strongest protest against the passage of this legislation. This Bill has been before the House for a considerable time; and it does not indicate fair-play that a Bill of such effect as this should be brought forward for second reading and committee after twelve o'clock on the last day but one of the session. The Bill is objectionable for the reasons that I have stated, and the time and manner of its being brought forward for passage is not an indication of good faith.
Does the hon. member not remember that all this was said two or three weeks ago, and that the matter was thoroughly discussed on the resolution. .

Perhaps most of what has been said was said on a former occasion. Then the minister saw fit to leave this Bill on the Order Paper until, as the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says, we have come to the closing hours of the session. It is now an early hour of the morning, with a small membership in the House. Many other members, had they been in the House, would add their protest to those already made.
After _ listening to the remarks of the hon. minister, I am more than ever convinced of the vicious character of this legislation. The hon. minister admitted that this Bill was intended to mean exactly what I thought it meant; that is to say, he proposes to make the exporter from the United States conform, so far as branding and marking is concerned, with the fruit grower in Canada.
Why not?

My hon. friend's own judgment ought to show him that that makes practically an insurmountable obstacle, so far as importing fruit from the United States is concerned. The fruit grower and packer in each state is com- pelled to pack and brand his fruit according to the laws and regulations of his state. He is primarily supposed to be catering to the trade of his own country, and therefore he considers its regulations. Suppose he was allowed by the laws of his state to adopt two systems of packing and branding for a particular grade of fruit, which is no more than the Canadian fruit grower is permitted to do. His chief customers are in his own country, but we in Canada are compelled to import fruit from the United States. By this legislation we are giving to the hon. minister or to the Mr. OLIVER
Governor in Council the power to say to the fruit exporter from the United States that, when his fruit crosses the international boundary, he must conform with the laws and regulations of the Dominion of Canada as to grading and branding. I think my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), who comes from a fruit district, ought to see the effect of such legislation. The grades, brands and markings used in the United States are different from ours. The hon. minister has admitted, from a practical standpoint, that this legislation is not necessary; that the bulk of the fruit coming from the United States comes in good packing, well packed and well graded. While the grades are not uniform with ours in that they are marked or named differently, nevertheless every Canadian importer of fruit from the United States knows exactly what quality of fruit to expect when he orders a certain brand.

Has the Canadian
exporter to conform with American laws?

Not by any means. I am sure of that, excepting that his fruit has to conform with the Canadian brands. The minister undertook to say that so far as the export of our beef is concerned it must conform to the legislation of the United States. Of course it must, so far as inspection is concerned. If it is bad meat, it is diseased, it cannot cross the international boundary, and be distributed in the United States. If we export our fruit, that fruit must conform to what the importer in another country knows to be the grade according to the Canadian brand. So, it is proper to see to it that fruit that comes from the United States marked according to American legislation, shall conform to the brand as fixed by that legislation. But that is a very different thing from what this Bill proposes which dictates what the brands shall be. What will be the effect of this legislation? A shipment of apples, for instance comes across the boundary graded according to the regulations on the American side where it was grown. The minister takes power under this Bill to compel the unpacking and regrading of these apples according to the grades fixed in Canada. The minister knows-he must know-that that is vicious legislation.
Mr. LANCASTER. But if the packer knew that is the law in Canada, would not he pack the fruit in the first place to conform to the law of the country in which he expected to sell? He would if he is not a fool, and if you want legislation for fools in the United States, it is no wonder you do not accept this Bill.

The hon. member must
know that fruit packed in Canada and fruit packed in the United States must _ conform to the laws of the country in which it is packed.
Yes, but if the packer is going to sell it in Canada he must conform to the laws of Canada.
Where is the fruit grower in the United States going to do his packing? He packs it in the United States and must pack it according to the laws of his own country.

As the hon. gentleman asks the question, the answer is that if the American packer seeks the Canadian market, he knows, what the hon. gentleman says everybody knows, that there is a law in Canada with regard to the packing of fruit, and he will pack it in accordance with that law, just as the Canadian packer will do.

The minister who sits beside the hon. member for Lincoln I am sure could enlighten him that in Canada as well as in the United States the fruit packer is not allowed to pack according to the laws of any country but his own.
There is no federal law on this subject similar to our own. This is done in the several states by associations or individuals very largely.

If I am correctly informed, the several * states regulate these matters. But the minister knows perfectly well the effect of state legislation there is the same as that of federal legislation in this country. The packer on either side must conform to the law under which he lives.
Would not that apply to the different states ? So, a packer in the United States could not sell outside of his own state according to the hon. gentleman's argument.

There is no legislation as between state and state such as we are proposing putting into effect, as between Canada and the United States. They certainly can ship their fruit from one state to another as they do from the United States to Canada, but if we adopt this legislation they will not be able to ship into, Canada.
The hon. gentleman is talking a lot of law about which he knows nothing.

The hon. member for
Lincoln may know a great deal of law, but instances have come under my own observation in which his knowledge has not been exactly plain to the ordinary layman.
Give us a little common sense, then, seeing your law is no good.

The hon. gentleman speaks of law, and may know something on that subject, but when it comes to common sense, so far as my observation goes, that
is rather beyond him. It is common sense and not legal technicalities that I am discussing. The hon. gentleman is versed in legal technicalities, perhaps, but not in practical affairs. I said that the Canadian fruit grower must conform to the law of his own country and cannot pack and grade his fruit differently even if he wants to meet the regulations as to grading and branding of any other state to which he is going to ship. The minister should take the member for Lincoln aside and enlighten him on these practical questions.
Does not the hon. gentleman know that Canadian apples shipped to New York state must conform in regard to inspection and marking with the laws of that state ?
They must conform to the grade that is required in this country.
No, I ask if he does not know that they must conform to the laws of the State of New York ?

So far as inspection is concerned, that is quite possible. But if there is a state of the Union that enacts legislation of the sort the hon. gentleman speaks of, it is outside my knowledge. I would like to see it before I would believe that such legislation exists in any state of the Union.
If the hon. gentleman had lived in the fruit-growing district as I have, he would know absolutely that this has been so for years. That is the fallacy of his whole argument.
I will take the hon. gentleman's word when he produces the proof.
That is your size.

The hon. gentleman says
he knows this; he ought to be able to submit the proofs.
I have lived there for thirty years, and that has been the law for twenty years.
Just the same as the law of Canada is to-day, and it does not require any change such as is proposed.
You are wrong again.

I think probably my hon. friend, with all his years of experience, may be mistaken as to legislation of New York state. 1 shall be glad to look into the matter if my hon. friend can furnish evidence that so far as marking is concerned we must employ the same marks as the fruit packers of the state of New York. Does my hon. friend say that?

Yes, if you are shipping to packers in New York state that is so, and has been so for years. The hon.
11961)

gentleman ought to have acquainted himself with the facts before taking up the time of the House in discussing this matter on false premises.

So far as taking up the time of the House is concerned, I have no apology to make to my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman takes up his own share of the time of the House, and I do not require any advice from him as to the time I shall take up in the discussion of any particular matter. My hon. friend gives his word as to a certain condition of affairs existing in New York 3tate; if he has information on the subject he ought to be able to prove his assertions. Whether or not that legislation does exist in New York state-does not affect this question one particle. Even if that legislation does exist in New York state, taking my hon. friend's word without proof, I say that this would be vicious legislation if the people of New York state were large importers of fruit, because we are, as is demonstrated by the blue books, very heavy exporters to the United States, and these regulations without the shadow of a doubt, would be a very great injury to that trade and a very great hindrance so far as obtaining fruit from the United States is concerned.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

On motion of Hon. Louis Coderre (Secretary of State), Bill No. 240, to amend the Public Archives Act, was read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair).

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Under the law placing the public archives under the Department of the Secretary of State, the Dominion archivist was accorded the rank and status of a deputy minister. Up to the present time certain duties in respect of the archives have been fulfilled by the Undersecretary of State, and it has been thought desirable that the Dominion archivist should assume the duties, as well as responsibility for and control over the finances of the archives. The Dominion -archivist is himself desirous that this change shall be effected, and the purpose of the amendment is to fulfil this common desire. Under this amendment all these duties will now be assumed by the Dominion archivist. Since I have been in charge of the Department of the Secretary of State, the desire has been very emphatically expressed by both Mr. Mulvey, the under Secretary of Sstate, and Dr. Doughty, Dominion archivist, that this amendment should be passed. Dr. Doughty would like to have control of his own finances, and Mr. Mulvey does not care to interfere in the finances of tie Do-Mr. LANCASTER.
minion archivist. That is the whole purpose of this amendment.
Does this create another deputy minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This does not create a
new deputy minister.	.

Last year Dr. Doughty, whose services as Dominion archivist we have been very fortunate to have, was given the rank and salary of a deputy minister, and this amendment has regard to the -administration of that branch of the Department of the Secretary of State. Dr. Doughty, I understand sends to the United States, England, France and other countries young men who are authorized to copy very interesting documents, and it is in order to avoid red tape that this -power is given him to administer the affairs of his branch under the department. I can assure my hon. friend the member for Carleton, knowing Dr. Doughty as I do know him, that no department of the Government is better administered than that branch of the Secretary of State known as the public archives.
Mr. -CARVELL: Does this mean the appointment of extra clerks? Certain duties now being performed by the under-Secretary of State are being handed over to the Dominion archivist, and I presume that) means the appointment of a staff of clerks.-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There may be an accountant. Whether the Government pays the present accountant of the Secretary of State for the work that he is now doing for the Archives branch, or pays another accountant, seems to me a matter of indifference.

If an accountant be
appointed for the Archives, will there be a reduction of the salary to that extent in the Secretary of State's office?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is to-day before
the department a request by Mr. Coulson, the accountant of the department, for relief, as he contends he has been overworked because he has been obliged to do the accounting of the public archives; for that he has been paid no more than he would -be entitled to as accountant of the Department of State. Whether we pay him an additional amount or whether we pay a separate accountant for the Archives seems to me to be a matter of indifference.

I suppose it is no use objecting, but it seems to me as if it was a case of the tail wagging the dog. The Civil Service is growing to such an extent in Ottawa that I do not know where the end will be. I have no fault to find with Dr. Doughty, who is a good man; but there is no doubt every move made means

more officials. The minister -will not say that it will reduce the cost in his own department; his own officials will receive as much as now, but a new set of officials will be created in the Archives branch. It seems to me that this Parliament is acting almost like a lot of children; all that is necessary is for someone to say: I am not getting enough salary, I ought to have promotion, and they devise some means by which a new office is created, a new deputy minister is provided for, and $15,000 or $20,000 expended,
Has the minister made choice of a successor to Mr. Roy, the very able assistant archivist who died the other day, and whose death is an irreparable loss to the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No action has been taken. Many applications have been made and I believe the best man will be chosen.

Mr. Roy, who was appointed by the late Government, was, of course, a well known Conservative. He was appointed because of his special ability as an archivist, he had made a special study of the archives and was known not only in Canada but in other countries. I hope my hon. friend in choosing his successor will make a similar choice, that is to say that he will have regard to the ability only of the person appointed and not to his political leanings.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There are no politics
in that.

I trust he will make
the best choice in the interest of the country.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.
